text:
0. Setup & Synthetic Clinical Cohort

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(pROC)
library(rsample)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(testthat)
library(gt)
library(jsonlite)
library(digest)
library(fs)

mod08_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mod08")
cap_dir <- file.path(mod08_dir, "capstone")
dir.create(cap_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

col_blue <- "#2563EB"
col_red  <- "#DC2626"
col_green <- "#16A34A"
col_gold <- "#D4A017"
col_purple <- "#B47CC7"
tier_colors <- c("Low" = col_blue, "Moderate" = col_green, "High" = col_gold, "Very High" = col_red)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.line        = element_line(colour = "grey40")
    )
)

SEED <- 42
set.seed(SEED)

sigmoid <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
avg_precision <- function(y, p) {
  ord <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
  y <- y[ord]; tp <- cumsum(y); prec <- tp / seq_along(y); rec <- tp / sum(y)
  sum(diff(c(0, rec)) * prec)
}
brier_score <- function(y, p) mean((p - y)^2)

N <- 3000
age   <- as.integer(pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 60, 15), 18), 90))
sex   <- sample(c("M", "F"), N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.48, 0.52))
race  <- sample(c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Other"), N, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.60, 0.18, 0.12, 0.06, 0.04))
payer <- sample(c("Medicare", "Medicaid", "Private", "Self-pay"), N, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.40, 0.22, 0.28, 0.10))
los   <- as.integer(pmin(pmax(rgamma(N, 2.5, scale = 1.8), 1), 30))
dm    <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.35)
hf    <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.22)
copd  <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.18)
smoking <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.25)
n_com <- dm + hf + copd
logit <- -3.2 + 0.6 * hf + 0.5 * dm + 0.3 * copd + 0.02 * (age - 60) +
  0.2 * as.integer(los > 7) + rnorm(N, 0, 0.3)
readmitted <- rbinom(N, 1, sigmoid(logit))
df <- tibble(
  age = age, sex = sex, race = race, payer = payer,
  los_days = los, diabetes = dm, hf = hf, copd = copd,
  smoking = smoking, n_comorb = n_com, readmitted = readmitted
)
FEATURES <- c("age", "los_days", "diabetes", "hf", "copd", "n_comorb")
split <- initial_split(df, prop = 0.8, strata = readmitted)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
df_tr <- train
df_te <- test
X_tr <- df_tr[FEATURES]; y_tr <- df_tr$readmitted
X_te <- df_te[FEATURES]; y_te <- df_te$readmitted
cat(sprintf("Capstone dataset: N=%d | Readmission: %.1f%% | Features: %d\n",
            N, mean(readmitted) * 100, length(FEATURES)))

Capstone dataset: N=3000 | Readmission: 7.0% | Features: 6

1. Training Run Log & Model Selection

predict_prob <- function(fit, X, type) {
  if (type == "glm") {
    as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = X, type = "response"))
  } else if (type == "ranger") {
    pred <- predict(fit, data = X)$predictions
    if (is.matrix(pred)) {
      cn <- colnames(pred)
      pred[, cn == "1" | cn == "TRUE"]
    } else pred
  } else {
    predict(fit, as.matrix(X))
  }
}

models_config <- list(
  LR_baseline = list(type = "glm", train = function() {
    w <- ifelse(y_tr == 1, sum(y_tr == 0) / max(sum(y_tr == 1), 1), 1)
    glm(readmitted ~ ., data = bind_cols(X_tr, readmitted = y_tr),
        family = binomial(), weights = w)
  }),
  GBM_v1 = list(type = "xgb", train = function() {
    xgb.train(
      params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
                    eval_metric = "auc"),
      data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(X_tr), label = y_tr),
      nrounds = 200, verbose = 0
    )
  }),
  GBM_v2_deep = list(type = "xgb", train = function() {
    xgb.train(
      params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", max_depth = 6, eta = 0.03,
                    subsample = 0.8, eval_metric = "auc"),
      data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(X_tr), label = y_tr),
      nrounds = 300, verbose = 0
    )
  })
)

run_log <- list()
fitted_models <- list()
fitted_probs <- list()
cat("Model training run log:\n")

Model training run log:

cat(sprintf("%-20s %8s %8s %8s %9s\n", "Run name", "AUC", "AP", "Brier", "Time(s)"))

Run name                  AUC       AP    Brier   Time(s)

cat(strrep("-", 55), "\n")

------------------------------------------------------- 

for (name in names(models_config)) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  fit <- models_config[[name]]$train()
  prob <- predict_prob(fit, X_te, models_config[[name]]$type)
  metrics <- list(
    auc   = as.numeric(pROC::auc(y_te, prob, quiet = TRUE)),
    ap    = avg_precision(y_te, prob),
    brier = brier_score(y_te, prob)
  )
  elapsed <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
  run_log[[length(run_log) + 1]] <- tibble(
    run_name = name, elapsed_s = round(elapsed, 2),
    auc = metrics$auc, ap = metrics$ap, brier = metrics$brier
  )
  fitted_models[[name]] <- fit
  fitted_probs[[name]] <- prob
  cat(sprintf("  %-18s %8.4f %8.4f %8.4f %9.2f\n",
              name, metrics$auc, metrics$ap, metrics$brier, elapsed))
}

Warning in eval(family$initialize): non-integer #successes in a binomial glm!


  LR_baseline          0.6644   0.1214   0.2286      0.02
  GBM_v1               0.5849   0.0970   0.0581      3.46

runs_df <- bind_rows(run_log)
best_name <- runs_df$run_name[which.max(runs_df$auc)]
best_model <- fitted_models[[best_name]]
best_type <- models_config[[best_name]]$type
best_prob_arr <- fitted_probs[[best_name]]
cat(sprintf("\nBest model: %s (AUC=%.4f)\n", best_name, max(runs_df$auc)))


Best model: LR_baseline (AUC=0.6644)

saveRDS(best_model, model_path)
write_json(runs_df, file.path(cap_dir, "run_log.json"), pretty = TRUE)

2. Data Provenance & Fairness

sha256_file <- function(path) digest::digest(file = path, algo = "sha256")

raw_csv <- file.path(cap_dir, "cohort.csv")
write_csv(df, raw_csv)
manifest <- list(
  created_at = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
  r_version  = paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
  files = list(cohort = list(
    path = raw_csv,
    source = "Synthetic (MIMIC-III inspired), seed=42",
    sha256 = sha256_file(raw_csv),
    n_rows = nrow(df), n_cols = ncol(df)
  ))
)
write_json(manifest, file.path(cap_dir, "MANIFEST.json"), pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)

auc_overall <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(y_te, best_prob_arr, quiet = TRUE))
fairness <- list()
for (spec in list(
  list(col = "race", groups = c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian")),
  list(col = "payer", groups = c("Medicare", "Medicaid", "Private", "Self-pay")),
  list(col = "sex", groups = c("M", "F"))
)) {
  for (grp in spec$groups) {
    mask <- df_te[[spec$col]] == grp
    if (sum(mask) < 20) next
    sub_y <- y_te[mask]; sub_p <- best_prob_arr[mask]
    if (n_distinct(sub_y) < 2) next
    auc_g <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(sub_y, sub_p, quiet = TRUE))
    fairness[[length(fairness) + 1]] <- tibble(
      Group = paste0(spec$col, "=", grp),
      N = sum(mask),
      AUC = round(auc_g, 4),
      Delta = round(auc_g - auc_overall, 4)
    )
  }
}
fairness_df <- bind_rows(fairness)

3. Automated Validation Tests

capstone_tests <- tryCatch(
  test_that("capstone model validation", {
    expect_gt(auc_overall, 0.65)
    expect_true(all(best_prob_arr >= 0) && all(best_prob_arr <= 1))
    X_high <- tibble(age = 80, los_days = 14, diabetes = 1, hf = 1, copd = 1, n_comorb = 3)
    X_low  <- tibble(age = 25, los_days = 1,  diabetes = 0, hf = 0, copd = 0, n_comorb = 0)
    p_high <- predict_prob(best_model, X_high, best_type)
    p_low  <- predict_prob(best_model, X_low, best_type)
    expect_gt(p_high, p_low)
    expect_false(any(is.na(best_prob_arr)))
    expect_gt(mean(y_te), 0.05)
    expect_lt(mean(y_te), 0.50)
  }),
  error = function(e) {
    cat("Capstone validation tests reported a failure:\n", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
    FALSE
  }
)

4. plumber Endpoint Simulation

simulate_api <- function(age, los_days, diabetes, hf, copd, patient_id = NULL) {
  if (!all(map_lgl(list(age, los_days, diabetes, hf, copd), is.numeric))) {
    return(list(error = "422 Unprocessable Entity", detail = "Invalid field types"))
  }
  if (!(18 <= age && age <= 90)) return(list(error = "422", detail = sprintf("age must be 18-90, got %s", age)))
  if (!(1 <= los_days && los_days <= 60)) return(list(error = "422", detail = "los_days must be 1-60"))
  X <- tibble(age = age, los_days = los_days, diabetes = diabetes,
              hf = hf, copd = copd, n_comorb = diabetes + hf + copd)
  prob <- as.numeric(predict_prob(best_model, X, best_type))[1]
  tier <- if (prob < 0.10) "Low" else if (prob < 0.20) "Moderate" else if (prob < 0.35) "High" else "Very High"
  list(
    patient_id = patient_id,
    readmission_probability = round(prob, 4),
    risk_tier = tier,
    model_version = "1.0.0",
    timestamp = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
  )
}

5. Publication Summary Figure (300 dpi)

# Step 5: Publication-quality summary figure (8 panels, 300 dpi)
roc_obj <- pROC::roc(y_te, best_prob_arr, quiet = TRUE)
roc_df <- tibble(fpr = 1 - roc_obj$specificities, tpr = roc_obj$sensitivities)

cal_df <- tibble(y = y_te, p = best_prob_arr) %>%
  mutate(bin = ntile(p, 10)) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  summarise(predicted = mean(p), observed = mean(y), .groups = "drop")

runs_long <- runs_df %>%
  select(run_name, auc, ap) %>%
  pivot_longer(-run_name, names_to = "metric", values_to = "score") %>%
  mutate(metric = recode(metric, auc = "AUC-ROC", ap = "Avg Precision"))

p_a <- ggplot(runs_long, aes(run_name, score, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.7), width = 0.65, colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", score)),
            position = position_dodge(0.7), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("AUC-ROC" = col_blue, "Avg Precision" = col_red)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score", title = "A  Model Comparison (Training Run Log)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 10, hjust = 1))

p_b <- ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = tpr), fill = col_red, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "1-Specificity", y = "Sensitivity",
       title = sprintf("B  ROC Curve (AUC=%.3f)", auc_overall))

p_c <- ggplot(cal_df, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = col_blue, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = col_blue, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Predicted", y = "Observed fraction",
       title = sprintf("C  Calibration Curve (Brier=%.3f)", brier_score(y_te, best_prob_arr)))

fair_sorted <- fairness_df %>% arrange(AUC) %>%
  mutate(col = if_else(abs(Delta) > 0.05, col_red, col_blue),
         Group = factor(Group, levels = Group))
p_d <- ggplot(fair_sorted, aes(Group, AUC, fill = col)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = auc_overall, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = auc_overall - 0.05, colour = "orange", linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.6, 0.9)) +
  labs(y = "AUC-ROC", title = "D  Fairness Analysis by Subgroup", x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 7))

tier_cut <- cut(best_prob_arr, c(0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.35, 1.01),
                labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Very High"))
tier_counts <- tibble(tier = tier_cut) %>% count(tier, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
p_e <- ggplot(tier_counts, aes(tier, n, fill = tier)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tier_colors) +
  labs(y = "N patients", title = "E  Risk Tier Distribution", x = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

df_te$risk_tier <- tier_cut
tier_readmit <- df_te %>%
  group_by(risk_tier) %>%
  summarise(rate = mean(readmitted) * 100, .groups = "drop")
p_f <- ggplot(tier_readmit, aes(risk_tier, rate, fill = risk_tier)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", rate)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tier_colors) +
  labs(y = "Actual readmission rate (%)", title = "F  Actual Rate by Predicted Tier", x = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

governance_items <- tibble(
  item = c(
    "Data MANIFEST.json with SHA-256",
    "packages.R / renv.lock (pinned)",
    "Pipeline.log recorded",

6. Deployment Narrative

DEPLOYMENT_NARRATIVE <- paste(
  c(
    "METHODS NARRATIVE",
    strrep("=", 60),
    "",
    sprintf("We developed and validated a 30-day hospital readmission prediction model"),
    sprintf("using a cohort of N=%s general medical-surgical patients (2019-2023).", format(N, big.mark = ",")),
    "",
    "FEATURE ENGINEERING: Six pre-discharge features were selected based on",
    "clinical plausibility and availability in the EHR at discharge:",
    "age, length of stay, diabetes, heart failure, COPD, and comorbidity count.",
    "",
    "MODEL TRAINING: Three models were evaluated: logistic regression (baseline),",
    "gradient boosting v1, and gradient boosting v2 with deeper trees. Models were",
    "compared on AUC-ROC, Average Precision, and Brier score on a 20% holdout test set.",
    "",
    sprintf("PERFORMANCE: Best model (%s) achieved AUC-ROC=%.4f and", best_name, auc_overall),
    sprintf("Average Precision=%.4f. Calibration was assessed with a calibration curve",
            avg_precision(y_te, best_prob_arr)),
    sprintf("(Brier score=%.4f).", brier_score(y_te, best_prob_arr)),
    "",
    "FAIRNESS: Performance was evaluated across sex, race/ethnicity, and payer subgroups.",
    sprintf("Maximum AUC disparity was %.4f (threshold: 0.05). %s",
            max(abs(fairness_df$Delta)),
            if (max(abs(fairness_df$Delta)) < 0.05) "No significant disparities detected." else "REVIEW REQUIRED."),

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.line        = element_line(colour = "grey40")
    )
)

set.seed(42)
N <- 2000
sigmoid <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
age  <- as.integer(pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 60, 15), 18), 90))
los  <- as.integer(pmin(pmax(rgamma(N, 2.5, scale = 1.8), 1), 30))
dm   <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.35)
hf   <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.22)
copd <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.18)
logit <- -3.2 + 0.6 * hf + 0.5 * dm + 0.3 * copd + 0.02 * (age - 60) +
  0.2 * as.integer(los > 7)
readmitted <- rbinom(N, 1, sigmoid(logit))
df <- tibble(age = age, los_days = los, diabetes = dm, hf = hf, copd = copd,
             readmitted = readmitted)
FEATURES <- c("age", "los_days", "diabetes", "hf", "copd")
split <- initial_split(df, prop = 0.8, strata = readmitted)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
X_tr <- train[FEATURES]; y_tr <- train$readmitted
X_te <- test[FEATURES];  y_te <- test$readmitted
model <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
                eval_metric = "auc"),
  data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(X_tr), label = y_tr),
  nrounds = 200, verbose = 0
)
auc <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(y_te, predict(model, as.matrix(X_te)), quiet = TRUE))
cat(sprintf("Test dataset: %d patients | AUC=%.4f\n", N, auc))

Test dataset: 2000 patients | AUC=0.5896

3. Unit Tests: Data Pipeline

# Unit tests for data pipeline and model functions
validate_features <- function(df, required_cols, age_col = "age", target_col = "readmitted") {
  errors <- character()
  missing <- setdiff(required_cols, names(df))
  if (length(missing)) errors <- c(errors, paste("Missing columns:", paste(missing, collapse = ", ")))
  if (age_col %in% names(df) && !all(df[[age_col]] >= 18 & df[[age_col]] <= 90)) {
    errors <- c(errors, paste(age_col, "values outside 18-90 range"))
  }
  if (target_col %in% names(df) && !all(df[[target_col]] %in% c(0, 1))) {
    errors <- c(errors, paste(target_col, "must be binary 0/1"))
  }
  errors
}

compute_positive_rate <- function(y) mean(y)

compute_smr <- function(observed, expected) {
  if (expected <= 0) stop("Expected must be positive")
  observed / expected
}

clean_age <- function(age_series, min_age = 18, max_age = 90) {
  pmin(pmax(age_series, min_age), max_age)
}

df_valid <- tibble(
  age = c(65, 45, 72), los_days = c(5, 3, 12),
  diabetes = c(1, 0, 1), hf = c(0, 0, 1), copd = c(0, 0, 1), readmitted = c(0, 0, 1)
)
df_invalid <- df_valid
df_invalid$age[1] <- 150

pipeline_results <- test_that("data pipeline validation", {
  expect_equal(validate_features(df_valid, c(FEATURES, "readmitted")), character(0))
  expect_true(any(grepl("age", validate_features(df_invalid, FEATURES), ignore.case = TRUE)))
  df_missing <- df_valid %>% select(-hf)
  expect_true(any(grepl("hf", validate_features(df_missing, FEATURES))))
  y <- c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0)
  rate <- compute_positive_rate(y)
  expect_gte(rate, 0)
  expect_lte(rate, 1)
  expect_equal(rate, 0.4, tolerance = 1e-5)
  expect_equal(compute_smr(observed = 8, expected = 5.0), 1.6, tolerance = 1e-5)
  expect_error(compute_smr(observed = 3, expected = 0))
  cleaned <- clean_age(c(15, 50, 100))
  expect_equal(min(cleaned), 18)
  expect_equal(max(cleaned), 90)
})

# Setup: install.packages('precommit'); precommit::use_precommit()

compute_code_metrics <- function(source_code) {
  parsed <- tryCatch(parse(text = source_code, keep.source = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(parsed, "error")) return(list(error = parsed$message))
  pd <- getParseData(parsed)
  n_fn <- sum(pd$token == "FUNCTION", na.rm = TRUE)
  lines <- strsplit(source_code, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  code_lines <- lines[nzchar(trimws(lines)) & !startsWith(trimws(lines), "#")]
  list(
    lines_of_code = length(code_lines),
    num_functions = n_fn,
    num_classes   = sum(grepl("R6Class|setClass", source_code)),
    comment_lines = sum(startsWith(trimws(lines), "#"))

8. Knowledge Check

A test checks auc > 0.65. The AUC is 0.66, so the test passes. Six months later a data bug makes AUC=0.67 look good but the data is corrupted. What additional tests would catch this?
Your CI pipeline takes 45 minutes to run. 12 developers each push 5 times/day. What optimisations reduce this to <10 minutes?
A property-based test found that age=18, los_days=1 all zeros returns prob=0.0001. Is this a bug?
Pre-commit hooks auto-format an R script (styler) and change 200 lines. How does this affect reproducibility?
Write a test that verifies the model’s AUC on a held-out test set is within 0.05 of the AUC logged in MLflow for the production model.


# Exercise 5 — MLflow AUC consistency test
test_model_auc_consistent_with_registry <- function(model_obj, X_test, y_test,
                                                    registry_path = file.path(mod08_dir, "model_registry.json"),
                                                    tolerance = 0.05) {
  if (!file.exists(registry_path)) {
    cat("SKIP: No model registry file found\n")
    return(TRUE)
  }
  registry <- fromJSON(registry_path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
  prod_versions <- Filter(function(v) identical(v$stage, "Production"), registry$version_history)
  if (!length(prod_versions)) {
    cat("SKIP: No production version in registry\n")
    return(TRUE)
  }
  registered_auc <- prod_versions[[length(prod_versions)]]$auc
  current_auc <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(y_test, predict(model_obj, as.matrix(X_test)), quiet = TRUE))
  auc_diff <- abs(current_auc - registered_auc)
  passed <- auc_diff <= tolerance
  cat(sprintf("Registry AUC : %.4f\n", registered_auc))
  cat(sprintf("Current AUC  : %.4f\n", current_auc))
  cat(sprintf("Difference   : %.4f (tolerance=%.2f)\n", auc_diff, tolerance))
  cat(sprintf("Test result  : %s\n", if (passed) "PASS" else "FAIL - model may have drifted!"))
  passed
}

tracker <- list(
  start_run = function(run_name) {
    tracker_env$current_run <- list(
      run_name = run_name, params = list(), metrics = list(), tags = list(),
      start_time = proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    )
  },
  log_param = function(key, value) tracker_env$current_run$params[[key]] <<- value,
  log_params = function(params) {
    for (k in names(params)) tracker_env$current_run$params[[k]] <<- params[[k]]
  },
  log_metric = function(key, value) {
    tracker_env$current_run$metrics[[key]] <<- round(as.numeric(value), 6)
  },
  log_metrics = function(metrics) {
    for (k in names(metrics)) tracker$log_metric(k, metrics[[k]])
  },
  set_tag = function(key, value) {
    tracker_env$current_run$tags[[key]] <<- as.character(value)
  },
  end_run = function() {
    tracker_env$current_run$duration_s <- round(
      proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - tracker_env$current_run$start_time, 2
    )
    tracker_env$runs[[length(tracker_env$runs) + 1]] <- tracker_env$current_run
    write_json(
      tracker_env$current_run,
      file.path(tracker_env$tracking_dir, paste0(tracker_env$current_run$run_name, ".json")),
      pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE
    )
  },
  get_runs_df = function() {
    map_dfr(tracker_env$runs, function(r) {
      params <- r$params; metrics <- r$metrics
      names(params) <- paste0("param.", names(params))
      names(metrics) <- paste0("metric.", names(metrics))
      bind_cols(
        tibble(run_name = r$run_name, duration_s = r$duration_s %||% 0),
        as_tibble(params), as_tibble(metrics)
      )
    })
  }
)

avg_precision <- function(y, p) {
  ord <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE)
  y <- y[ord]
  tp <- cumsum(y)
  prec <- tp / seq_along(y)
  rec  <- tp / sum(y)
  # step-wise PR-AUC
  sum(diff(c(0, rec)) * prec)
}
brier_score <- function(y, p) mean((p - y)^2)

predict_prob <- function(fit, X, type) {
  if (type == "glm") {
    as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = X, type = "response"))
  } else if (type == "ranger") {
    pred <- predict(fit, data = X)$predictions
    if (is.matrix(pred)) pred[, colnames(pred) == "1" | colnames(pred) == "TRUE"] else pred
  } else if (type == "xgb") {
    predict(fit, as.matrix(X))
  }
}

train_glm <- function(C) {
  w <- ifelse(y_tr == 1, sum(y_tr == 0) / max(sum(y_tr == 1), 1), 1)

      data = bind_cols(X_tr, readmitted = y_tr),

text:
8. Knowledge Check

You log 50 metrics per run. How do you decide which metrics are PRIMARY for model selection?
MLflow Model Registry has three stages: Staging, Production, Archived. What process should gate promotion from Staging to Production in a clinical context?
A new model has AUC=0.79 vs production model AUC=0.77. Should you always promote? What other factors matter?
Your MLflow database grows to 10GB after 6 months. What’s your data management strategy?
Implement a model drift detector: log weekly AUC scores and alert when AUC drops >0.03 below the baseline.


# Exercise 5 — Model drift detection
set.seed(42)
weeks <- 1:12
baseline_auc <- 0.780
weekly_aucs <- sapply(weeks, function(w) {
  if (w <= 8) baseline_auc + rnorm(1, 0, 0.01)
  else baseline_auc - 0.005 * (w - 8) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.01)
})
DRIFT_THRESHOLD <- baseline_auc - 0.03
drift_weeks <- weeks[weekly_aucs < DRIFT_THRESHOLD]

drift_df <- tibble(week = weeks, auc = weekly_aucs, drift = week %in% drift_weeks)
p_drift <- ggplot(drift_df, aes(week, auc)) +
  geom_rect(
    data = filter(drift_df, drift),
    aes(xmin = week - 0.4, xmax = week + 0.4, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = col_red, alpha = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = col_blue, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = drift, colour = drift), size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_auc, colour = col_green, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = DRIFT_THRESHOLD, colour = col_red, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = col_blue, "TRUE" = col_red)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 6)) +
  labs(
    x = "Week", y = "AUC-ROC",
    title = "Model Performance Drift Monitoring\n(red markers = drift alert triggered)",
    colour = "Alert", shape = "Alert"
  )
print(p_drift)







cat("Drift alerts triggered in weeks:", paste(drift_weeks, collapse = ", "), "\n")

    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.line        = element_line(colour = "grey40")
    )
)

set.seed(42)
N <- 2000
df <- tibble(
  patient_id = sprintf("PT-%05d", seq_len(N) - 1),
  age        = as.integer(pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 60, 15), 18), 90)),
  los_days   = as.integer(pmin(pmax(rgamma(N, 2.5, scale = 1.8), 1), 30)),
  diabetes   = rbinom(N, 1, 0.35),
  hf         = rbinom(N, 1, 0.22),
  smoking    = rbinom(N, 1, 0.25),
  payer      = sample(
    c("Medicare", "Medicaid", "Private", "Self-pay"),
    N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.40, 0.22, 0.28, 0.10)
  )
)
sigmoid <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
logit <- -3.2 + 0.6 * df$hf + 0.5 * df$diabetes + 0.02 * (df$age - 60) +
  0.2 * as.integer(df$los_days > 7)
df$readmitted <- rbinom(N, 1, sigmoid(logit))
cat(sprintf("Dataset: %d x %d | Readmission rate: %.1f%%\n",
            nrow(df), ncol(df), mean(df$readmitted) * 100))

2. Quarto Document Structure
A .qmd file is a Markdown file with YAML front matter and executable code chunks. This notebook is a Quarto document for R: you are looking at the same format you will use for journal-ready reports.
---                          # YAML front matter (metadata)
title: "Report Title"
format: html
engine: knitr

## Section                   # Markdown content

```{r}
#| label: fig-roc            # Cross-referenceable label
#| fig-cap: "ROC Curve"      # Caption
plot_roc_curve()
```

See @fig-roc for the discrimination results.   # Auto-numbered cross-ref
Key Quarto advantages over R Markdown / notebooks: - Clean separation of code and output - Native multi-format (HTML/PDF/Word) from same source - Built-in bibliography (.bib) support - Cross-references, callouts, panel layouts - Version-control friendly (.qmd is plain text) - Knitr engine is first-class for R ({r} chunks, echo, cache, fig-cap)
Chunk options you will use constantly:



Option
Purpose




#\| label: fig-roc
Cross-reference target (@fig-roc)


#\| fig-cap:
Figure caption


#\| tbl-cap:
Table caption


#\| echo: false
Hide code in the rendered report


#\| cache: true
Skip re-running unchanged chunks


#\| fig-width: / #\| fig-height:
Figure size in inches


#\| message: false
Suppress package startup messages

4. Publication-Quality Figures (300 dpi)

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(df, prop = 0.8, strata = readmitted)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

fit <- glm(
  readmitted ~ age + los_days + diabetes + hf + smoking,
  data = train, family = binomial()
)
prob <- predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response")
auc  <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(test$readmitted, prob, quiet = TRUE))
roc_obj <- pROC::roc(test$readmitted, prob, quiet = TRUE)
roc_df <- tibble(fpr = 1 - roc_obj$specificities, tpr = roc_obj$sensitivities)

# Panel A — ROC
p_a <- ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = tpr), fill = col_red, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "1 - Specificity", y = "Sensitivity",
       title = "A  ROC Curve", subtitle = sprintf("AUC = %.3f", auc))

# Panel B — Score distribution
score_df <- tibble(prob = prob, readmitted = factor(test$readmitted,
                     labels = c("Not readmitted", "Readmitted")))
p_b <- ggplot(score_df, aes(prob, fill = readmitted)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 25, alpha = 0.65,
                 position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_red)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted probability", y = "Density",
       title = "B  Score Distribution", fill = NULL)

# Panel C — Readmission by factor
baseline <- mean(df$readmitted) * 100
factor_rates <- tibble(
  feature = c("HF", "Diabetes", "Smoking", "LOS>7d", "Age>70"),
  rate = c(
    mean(df$readmitted[df$hf == 1]),
    mean(df$readmitted[df$diabetes == 1]),
    mean(df$readmitted[df$smoking == 1]),
    mean(df$readmitted[df$los_days > 7]),
    mean(df$readmitted[df$age > 70])
  ) * 100
) %>%
  mutate(col = if_else(rate > baseline + 3, col_red, col_blue))
p_c <- ggplot(factor_rates, aes(rate, reorder(feature, rate), fill = col)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = "30-day readmission rate (%)", y = NULL,
       title = "C  Readmission by Factor")

# Panel D — Payer analysis
payer_rates <- df %>%
  group_by(payer) %>%
  summarise(rate = mean(readmitted) * 100, .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(rate)) %>%
  mutate(payer = factor(payer, levels = payer),
         col = c(col_red, col_gold, col_blue, col_green))
p_d <- ggplot(payer_rates, aes(payer, rate, fill = col)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", rate)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Readmission rate (%)", title = "D  Readmission by Payer") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1))

# Panel E — Feature importance (log-odds coefficients)
coefs <- broom::tidy(fit) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(col = if_else(estimate > 0, col_red, col_blue))
p_e <- ggplot(coefs, aes(estimate, reorder(term, estimate), fill = col)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = "Log-odds coefficient", y = NULL, title = "E  Model Coefficients")

# Panel F — LOS distribution
p_f <- ggplot(df, aes(los_days, fill = factor(readmitted,
                     labels = c("Not readmitted", "Readmitted")))) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20, alpha = 0.6,
                 position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_red)) +
  labs(x = "Length of Stay (days)", y = "Density",
       title = "F  LOS Distribution", fill = NULL)

fig1 <- (p_a | p_b | p_c) / (p_d | p_e | p_f) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "30-Day Hospital Readmission Analysis Report",
    subtitle = "Figure 1: Key Results Summary"
  )
print(fig1)

5. Programmatic Table 1

# Generate publication-ready Table 1 (patient characteristics)
table1_row_continuous <- function(df_all, col, group_col = "readmitted", label = NULL) {
  label <- label %||% col
  overall <- sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(df_all[[col]]), sd(df_all[[col]]))
  g0 <- df_all[[col]][df_all[[group_col]] == 0]
  g1 <- df_all[[col]][df_all[[group_col]] == 1]
  p  <- wilcox.test(g0, g1, alternative = "two.sided")$p.value
  tibble(
    Variable = label, Overall = overall,
    `Not Readmitted` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(g0), sd(g0)),
    Readmitted = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(g1), sd(g1)),
    `p-value` = sprintf("%.3f", p)
  )
}

table1_row_binary <- function(df_all, col, group_col = "readmitted", label = NULL) {
  label <- label %||% col
  overall <- sprintf("%.1f%%", mean(df_all[[col]]) * 100)
  g0 <- df_all[[col]][df_all[[group_col]] == 0]
  g1 <- df_all[[col]][df_all[[group_col]] == 1]
  ct <- table(df_all[[col]], df_all[[group_col]])
  p  <- chisq.test(ct)$p.value
  tibble(
    Variable = label, Overall = overall,
    `Not Readmitted` = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean(g0) * 100),
    Readmitted = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean(g1) * 100),
    `p-value` = sprintf("%.3f", p)
  )
}

table1 <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Variable = "N", Overall = as.character(nrow(df)),
    `Not Readmitted` = as.character(sum(df$readmitted == 0)),
    Readmitted = as.character(sum(df$readmitted == 1)),
    `p-value` = ""
  ),
  table1_row_continuous(df, "age", "readmitted", "Age (years), mean (SD)"),
  table1_row_continuous(df, "los_days", "readmitted", "Length of stay (days), mean (SD)"),
  table1_row_binary(df, "diabetes", "readmitted", "Diabetes, n (%)"),
  table1_row_binary(df, "hf", "readmitted", "Heart failure, n (%)"),
  table1_row_binary(df, "smoking", "readmitted", "Current smoker, n (%)")
)

title: Geostatistical Risk Analysis
section: 2. Indicator Kriging for Environmental Health Risk
text:
2. Indicator Kriging for Environmental Health Risk
Indicator kriging (IK) is a non-parametric geostatistical method. After an indicator transformation of a continuous variable at one or more pre-defined thresholds, ordinary kriging of the 0/1 indicators maps the probability of exceeding those thresholds. That probability surface is directly useful for regulatory and public-health decisions.
IK can also reconstruct an entire cumulative distribution function (CDF) at unsampled locations. The mean of that CDF (the E-type estimate) is then an estimate of concentration after the upper and lower tails have been modelled (Goovaerts, 2009). CDF-based IK is attractive when the raw distribution is strongly skewed: log-transforms and other parametric estimators are easily dominated by extreme values.
In R, gstat implements indicator kriging of binary fields. There is still no CRAN package that builds E-type estimates from IK CDFs. That step is available in classical geostatistical software such as GSLIB and SGeMS. AUTO-IK (Goovaerts, 2009) automates GSLIB routines for threshold selection, indicator variogram modelling, prediction of probability distributions on regular or irregular grids, and estimation of the mean and variance of those distributions.
Ordinary kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of a spatially distributed variable. At an unsampled location \(\mathbf{s}_0\):
\[
\hat{Z}(\mathbf{s}_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i Z(\mathbf{s}_i)
\]
where \(Z(\mathbf{s}_i)\) are observed values and the weights \(\lambda_i\) minimise prediction variance subject to \(\sum_i \lambda_i = 1\).
IK applies the same estimator to a threshold indicator. For a cut-off \(z_c\):
\[
I(\mathbf{s}_i; z_c) =
  \begin{cases}
    1 & \text{if } Z(\mathbf{s}_i) > z_c \\
    0 & \text{otherwise}
  \end{cases}
\]
Kriging \(I(\mathbf{s}_i; z_c)\) estimates the conditional exceedance probability:
\[
\mathbb{P}[Z(\mathbf{s}_0) > z_c \mid \text{data}] \approx \hat{I}(\mathbf{s}_0; z_c) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i I(\mathbf{s}_i; z_c)
\]







Application
Why IK helps




Regulatory compliance
Map P(As > 10 µg/L) against the WHO guideline


National standards
Map P(As > 50 µg/L) against the Bangladesh drinking-water standard


Skewed distributions
Arsenic is strongly right-skewed; log-transforms distort tail behaviour


Censored data
Detection-limit samples can be handled before indicator coding



This notebook follows the classic BGS Bangladesh arsenic workflow:

Convert arsenic concentrations to indicators at 10 and 50 µg/L
Compute and model indicator semivariograms
Predict exceedance probabilities by indicator kriging
Map those probabilities on a national prediction grid

3.1 Handle detection limits
About 27.7% of sampled wells had arsenic below the instrumental detection limit of 0.5 µg/L (hydride generation–atomic fluorescence spectrometry) and 2.5% below 6.0 µg/L (hydride generation–ICP-AES). Following the BGS protocol, values below a detection limit are assigned half the equipment detection limit (0.25 or 3.0 µg/L). Many records in this file are already stored at those half-DL values; remaining readings reported exactly at 0.5 or 6.0 µg/L are converted here.

as_raw <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(df$As)))

# Half-DL substitution: HG-AFS (0.5 → 0.25) and HG-ICP-AES (6.0 → 3.0)
df$As_ppb <- case_when(
  is.na(as_raw)              ~ NA_real_,
  as_raw == 0.5              ~ 0.25,
  as_raw == 6.0              ~ 3.0,
  TRUE                       ~ as_raw
)

n_dl_icp <- sum(as_raw == 6.0, na.rm = TRUE)

n_half_icp <- sum(df$As_ppb == 3.0, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Geostatistical Risk Analysis
text:
8. Indicator Semivariograms
The semivariogram quantifies how spatial similarity decays with distance \(h\):
\[
\gamma(h) = \frac{1}{2N(h)} \sum_{i,j;\ |\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{s}_j| \approx h} \bigl[ Z(\mathbf{s}_i) - Z(\mathbf{s}_j) \bigr]^2
\]
An indicator variogram applies the same formula to \(I(\mathbf{s}; z_c)\). It describes the spatial continuity of high-risk vs low-risk zones rather than of concentration itself.
gstat cannot krige coincident locations, so we drop zero-distance pairs with zerodist() (the original IK workflow). Initial exponential parameters are set by eye, then refined by weighted least squares — the same vgm() / fit.variogram() sequence as the source notebook.

# Coincident boreholes: keep the first of each zerodist pair
ik_sp <- as(ik_sf, "Spatial")
zd <- zerodist(ik_sp)
n_coinc <- if (is.null(nrow(zd))) 0 else nrow(zd)
if (n_coinc > 0) {
  ik_sp <- ik_sp[-zd[, 1], ]
}
ik_sf <- st_as_sf(ik_sp)
mf <- st_drop_geometry(ik_sf)

cat(sprintf("Unique sample locations after zerodist(): %s (dropped %d coincident points)\n",
            format(nrow(ik_sf), big.mark = ","), n_coinc))

Unique sample locations after zerodist(): 3,420 (dropped 115 coincident points)

# Experimental indicator variograms (gstat defaults: cutoff ≈ 1/3 bounding-box diagonal)
v10 <- variogram(ik_10 ~ 1, data = ik_sf)
v50 <- variogram(ik_50 ~ 1, data = ik_sf)

# Initial exponential model set by eye, then WLS fit
m10 <- vgm(psill = 0.15, model = "Exp", range = 40000, nugget = 0.05)
m50 <- vgm(psill = 0.15, model = "Exp", range = 40000, nugget = 0.05)
m_f_10 <- fit.variogram(v10, m10)
m_f_50 <- fit.variogram(v50, m50)

cat("Fitted indicator variogram  As > 10 µg/L:\n")

plot_variogram <- function(v_emp, v_fit, title) {
  h_max <- max(v_emp$dist, na.rm = TRUE)
  h <- seq(0, h_max, length.out = 300)
  v_line <- variogramLine(v_fit, dist_vector = h)
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = v_emp, aes(dist, gamma), size = 2, shape = 19) +
    geom_line(data = v_line, aes(dist, gamma), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Distance (m)", y = "Semivariance", title = title)
}

print(
  plot_variogram(v10, m_f_10, "Indicator variogram\nAs > 10 µg/L") |
    plot_variogram(v50, m_f_50, "Indicator variogram\nAs > 50 µg/L")
)

text:
9. Cross-Validation
We run 5-fold cross-validation (gstat::krige.cv(..., nfold = 5)), the same procedure as in the original IK notebook (described there as leave-one-out in spirit: hold out a fold, predict P(indicator = 1) from the remaining points, compare with the observed 0/1). Predicted probabilities are then clipped to \([0, 1]\) — kriging of indicators is not guaranteed to stay inside that interval.

cv_10 <- krige.cv(ik_10 ~ 1, locations = ik_sf, model = m_f_10, nfold = 5, verbose = FALSE)
cv_50 <- krige.cv(ik_50 ~ 1, locations = ik_sf, model = m_f_50, nfold = 5, verbose = FALSE)

report_cv <- function(name, pred, obs) {
  brier <- mean((pred - obs)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("As > %s: Brier score = %.4f | pred range [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
              name, brier, min(pred, na.rm = TRUE), max(pred, na.rm = TRUE)))
}

report_cv("50 µg/L", cv_50$var1.pred, cv_50$observed)

cv_map <- function(cv, title) {
  xy_cv <- st_coordinates(st_as_sf(cv))
  plot_df <- tibble(
    x     = xy_cv[, 1],
    y     = xy_cv[, 2],
    obs   = as.integer(cv$observed > 0.5),
    pred  = cv$var1.pred
  )
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = bd, fill = NA, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(
      data = plot_df,
      aes(x, y, colour = factor(obs), size = 0.4 + 1.6 * pred),
      alpha = 0.65, stroke = 0
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("0" = "#16A34A", "1" = "#DC2626"), guide = "none") +
    scale_size_identity() +
    labs(
      title = title, x = "Easting (m)", y = "Northing (m)",
      subtitle = "Actual indicator: green / red = FALSE / TRUE; size ∝ predicted probability"
    ) +
    coord_sf()
}

print(
  cv_map(cv_10, "Probability of TRUE indicator (10 µg/L)") |
    cv_map(cv_50, "Probability of TRUE indicator (50 µg/L)")
)

text:
11. Probability Maps
The original workflow converted the kriging output to a raster (rasterFromXYZ) and plotted it with rasterVis::levelplot() using a blue–green–yellow–red ramp. We build the same surface with geom_tile on the 5 km grid.

probability_surface <- function(grid_df, value_col, title) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(
      data = grid_df,
      aes(x, y, fill = .data[[value_col]]),
      width = 5000, height = 5000
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = bd, fill = NA, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.25) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      name = "Probability",
      colours = ik_colours,
      limits = c(0, 1)
    ) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Easting (m)", y = "Northing (m)") +
    coord_sf() +
    theme_map() +
    theme(
      axis.title = element_text(size = 9),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.position = "right"
    )
}

print(
  probability_surface(grid_out, "p_as_gt_10", "Probability As > 10 µg/L") |
    probability_surface(grid_out, "p_as_gt_50", "Probability As > 50 µg/L")
)

title: Geostatistical Risk Analysis
text:
13. Interpretation & Health Policy Context
Key findings from indicator kriging:

IK maps where groundwater is likely unsafe, not only where boreholes were drilled — essential because sample density is uneven.
The 10 µg/L (WHO) surface is more extensive than the 50 µg/L (Bangladesh) surface, as expected from the stricter guideline.
Ordinary kriging of indicators can produce probabilities slightly outside \([0, 1]\); clipping after prediction is standard.
Cross-validation Brier scores summarise calibration; lower is better.
gstat delivers the probability maps; E-type concentration estimates would require multiple thresholds and CDF reconstruction (AUTO-IK / GSLIB / SGeMS).

Limitations:

IK assumes stationarity of the indicator semivariogram.
Half-DL substitution (0.25 / 3.0 µg/L) does not affect the 10 and 50 µg/L indicators, but it would matter for a full IK CDF.
A single exponential model is a simplification; nested structures or anisotropy can be added if the empirical variogram warrants it.

References:

Goovaerts P. (2009). AUTO-IK: a geostatistical program for indicator kriging. Environ Sci Technol.
BGS Bangladesh arsenic survey: bgs.ac.uk groundwater health data

title: Geostatistical Risk Analysis
text:
14. Knowledge Check

Why is indicator kriging preferred over ordinary kriging of log-arsenic when the goal is a regulatory exceedance map?
What does a predicted probability of 0.7 at an unmonitored grid cell mean for a household relying on a local tube well?
Why does gstat require zerodist() (or equivalent) before kriging, and what would happen if coincident points were left in?
The original notebook used an exponential model with vgm(0.15, "Exp", 40000, 0.05) as a starting guess. How would you check whether that model is adequate for the 50 µg/L indicator?
If the government wanted to prioritise well testing, how would you use the P(As > 50 µg/L) map together with the district table to rank districts?
Extend the analysis: add a third threshold (e.g. 200 µg/L) and compare the spatial pattern of severe poisoning risk. What extra step would AUTO-IK take that this notebook does not?

text:
3. Spatial Cluster Detection (Scan Statistic)
Poisson scan on diabetes: this extract has no total population, so uninsured count (a CHR measure that scales with county size) is the working at-risk denominator. Observed = prevalence × n; expected is n-weighted national mean (O/E = SPR).
For speed on 3,108 counties the search is limited to the k = 150 nearest centroids and B = 49 Monte Carlo permutations (Python used k = 500, B = 99). Windows are further capped at 15% of total expected count.

n_atrisk <- pmax(gdf$n_uninsured, 1)
prev <- gdf$diabetes_prev / 100
o <- prev * n_atrisk
e <- n_atrisk * (sum(o) / sum(n_atrisk))
e <- e * (sum(o) / sum(e))
Otot <- sum(o); Etot <- sum(e)
gdf$observed <- o
gdf$expected <- e
df$observed <- o
df$expected <- e

xy <- suppressWarnings(st_coordinates(st_centroid(gdf)))
MAXWIN <- 150
knn <- knearneigh(xy, k = MAXWIN - 1)
NB <- cbind(seq_len(N), knn$nn)

scan_max <- function(ovec, return_arg = FALSE) {
  o_win <- matrix(ovec[NB], nrow = N, ncol = MAXWIN)
  e_win <- matrix(e[NB], nrow = N, ncol = MAXWIN)
  Oz <- o_win; Ez <- e_win
  for (j in 2:MAXWIN) {
    Oz[, j] <- Oz[, j - 1] + o_win[, j]
    Ez[, j] <- Ez[, j - 1] + e_win[, j]
  }
  Oout <- Otot - Oz
  Eout <- Etot - Ez
  llr <- ifelse(Oz > 0, Oz * log(Oz / pmax(Ez, 1e-12)), 0) +
    ifelse(Oout > 0, Oout * log(Oout / pmax(Eout, 1e-12)), 0)
  keep <- is.finite(llr) & ((Oz / Ez) > (Oout / Eout)) & (Ez <= 0.15 * Etot)
  llr[!keep] <- -Inf
  if (!return_arg) return(max(llr))
  f <- which.max(llr)
  list(llr = llr[f], center = ((f - 1) %% N) + 1, k = ((f - 1) %/% N) + 1)
}

cat("Running scan statistic...\n")

Running scan statistic...

best <- scan_max(o, return_arg = TRUE)
best_in <- NB[best$center, seq_len(best$k)]
Oc <- sum(o[best_in]); Ec <- sum(e[best_in])
RR <- (Oc / Ec) / ((Otot - Oc) / (Etot - Ec))

n_perm <- 49
set.seed(11)
mc <- numeric(n_perm)
p_mult <- e / Etot
Otot_int <- as.integer(round(Otot))
for (b in seq_len(n_perm)) {
  Op <- as.numeric(rmultinom(1, Otot_int, p_mult))
  mc[b] <- scan_max(Op, return_arg = FALSE)
}
p_scan <- (sum(mc >= best$llr) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)

gdf$in_scan_cluster <- seq_len(N) %in% best_in

beta_hat  <- smr_mean / extra_var

quintile_score <- function(v, higher_is_worse = TRUE) {
  brks <- quantile(v, 0:5 / 5, na.rm = TRUE, type = 7)
  q <- as.numeric(cut(v, breaks = brks, include.lowest = TRUE,
                      labels = FALSE, duplicates = "drop"))
  if (higher_is_worse) q else 6 - q
}

gdf$cdi <- (
  quintile_score(gdf$diabetes_prev) +
    quintile_score(gdf$pct_obesity) +
    quintile_score(gdf$food_env_index, higher_is_worse = FALSE) +
    quintile_score(gdf$pct_exercise, higher_is_worse = FALSE) +
    quintile_score(gdf$access_2sfca, higher_is_worse = FALSE)
) / 5
gdf$cdi_cat <- cut(
  gdf$cdi, breaks = c(0, 2, 3, 4, 5.1),
  labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Very High")
)

text:
8. Methods Narrative Template

Spatial Epidemiology Methods
We conducted a county-level (N=3,108; CONUS + DC) spatial analysis of adult diabetes prevalence, metabolic and food-environment risk factors, and primary-care access. County Health Rankings and CDC diabetes prevalence were joined to NAD83 Albers county polygons (EPSG:5070). Standardised prevalence ratios (SPR) were computed as each county’s rate divided by the national mean. Empirical Bayes (Gamma-Poisson) smoothing used the CHR uninsured count as a working at-risk denominator to stabilise SPR estimates in small counties.
Spatial autocorrelation was assessed using Global Moran’s I with queen-contiguity weights, evaluated against 499 permutation-based null replicates. Local spatial clusters were identified with LISA (p<0.05), and disease hot spots confirmed with the Kulldorff circular scan statistic (B=49 Monte Carlo permutations, k=150 nearest-neighbour windows, 15% maximum expected-count window).
Diabetes prevalence was regressed on obesity, share aged 65+, access to exercise opportunities, and the food environment index using OLS and a spatial lag model (SLM; lagsarlm). Primary-care access was quantified with the Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (2SFCA) method using PCP counts as supply, uninsured counts as need-weighted demand, a 100 km catchment, and distance-decay power of 2.
A Compound Disadvantage Index (CDI) was constructed by averaging quintile scores across diabetes prevalence, obesity, food environment (inverted), exercise access (inverted), and 2SFCA access, identifying counties bearing multiple simultaneous burdens. All analyses used R (sf, spdep, spatialreg, ggplot2).

title: Environmental Epidemiology
text:
1. Setup
This section is dedicated to the setup for the environmental epidemiology analysis. It loads sf, gstat, ggplot2, and dplyr, sets visualisation defaults, and establishes a random seed for reproducibility. Spatial and geostatistical parameters (number of sampling points, spatial range, and variance for simulated pollution fields) are defined here.
The workflow is point-referenced (geostatistical simulation over CONUS), as a companion to the areal (county) simulation used elsewhere in Module 07. Sampling locations (air-quality monitors / survey sites) are placed at random points on US land. The PM2.5 signal and an unmeasured spatial confounder are drawn as true Gaussian random fields with an exponential covariance (known range + partial sill); PM2.5 is then observed with a nugget (measurement error). The same PM2.5 → CVD exposure-response is used as in the areal version (TRUE_PM25 = 2.5).
This gives data that (a) yields a recoverable variogram, and (b) exposes measurement-error attenuation of the exposure-response.

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gstat)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(42)
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mod07")
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
)

theme_map <- function() {
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0.5),
      legend.position = "right"
    )
}

# 1000 is safer for tutorial render (Cholesky is N×N). Python used 2000.
N_POINTS   <- 1000
RANGE_PM   <- 200.0    # PM2.5 field: exponential range parameter (km); eff. range ~3x
PSILL_PM   <- 4.0      # PM2.5 field: partial sill (spatial variance -> SD ~2 µg/m³)
NUGGET_SD  <- 1.5      # measurement error SD (µg/m³)
RANGE_RISK <- 350.0    # spatial-confounder field range (km)
TRUE_PM25  <- 2.5      # true exposure-response: 1 µg/m³ -> 2.5 CVD deaths/100k

county_shapes <- st_read("Data/US_COUNTY.shp", quiet = TRUE)
county_shapes$FIPS <- as.integer(county_shapes$FIPS)
# Shannon County SD (46113) was renamed Oglala Lakota (46102)
county_shapes$FIPS[county_shapes$FIPS == 46113] <- 46102

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Sample point locations on US land (inherit county context via join)
#    Area-weighted counties + jitter inside polygons (faster than st_sample
#    on a CONUS union, and faster than 2000-point rejection sampling).
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
areas <- as.numeric(st_area(county_shapes))
pick <- sample.int(nrow(county_shapes), N_POINTS, replace = TRUE, prob = pmax(areas, 1))

crs_albers <- st_crs(county_shapes)
place_in_poly <- function(geom) {
  cen <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(geom))[1, ]
  bb <- st_bbox(geom)
  sx <- max((bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"]) / 6, 1)
  sy <- max((bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"]) / 6, 1)
  for (i in 1:15) {
    xy <- c(cen[1] + rnorm(1, 0, sx), cen[2] + rnorm(1, 0, sy))
    pt <- st_sfc(st_point(xy), crs = crs_albers)
    if (as.logical(st_within(pt, geom, sparse = FALSE))) return(pt[[1]])
  }
  st_centroid(geom)[[1]]
}

pt_geoms <- lapply(pick, function(i) place_in_poly(county_shapes$geometry[i]))
pts <- st_sf(
  tibble(
    point_id = sprintf("P%04d", seq_len(N_POINTS) - 1),
    FIPS     = sprintf("%05d", county_shapes$FIPS[pick]),
    state    = county_shapes$STATE[pick],
    county   = county_shapes$COUNTY[pick]
  ),
  geometry = st_sfc(pt_geoms, crs = st_crs(county_shapes))
)

xy  <- st_coordinates(pts)
ll  <- st_transform(pts, 4326)
lon <- st_coordinates(ll)[, 1]
lat <- st_coordinates(ll)[, 2]
N   <- nrow(pts)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Gaussian random fields via exponential covariance
#    C(h) = psill * exp(-h / range_km), with h in km from Albers metres
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Dkm <- as.matrix(dist(xy)) / 1000

grf <- function(range_km, psill) {
  C <- psill * exp(-Dkm / range_km)
  diag(C) <- diag(C) + 1e-6 * psill
  # R chol() returns upper U with U'U = C; Python cholesky is lower L
  as.numeric(t(chol(C)) %*% rnorm(N))
}

field_pm   <- grf(RANGE_PM,   PSILL_PM)
field_risk <- grf(RANGE_RISK, 1.0)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. PM2.5 (signal + nugget), covariates, spatial confounder
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
pm25_base <- 8 + 4 * (lon - min(lon)) / (max(lon) - min(lon))   # W->E trend
pm25_true <- pmin(pmax(pm25_base + field_pm, 3), 30)            # latent signal
pm25      <- pmin(pmax(pm25_true + rnorm(N, 0, NUGGET_SD), 3), 30)  # measured

pct_poverty  <- 10 + 8 * rbeta(N, 2, 5) + 3 * sin(lon / 20)
population   <- as.integer(rlnorm(N, 10.5, 1.0))
spatial_risk <- as.numeric(scale(field_risk))                   # unmeasured confounder

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Outcome  (true exposure-response: 1 µg/m³ -> 2.5 CVD deaths/100k)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
cvd_rate <- 160 + 1.2 * pct_poverty + TRUE_PM25 * pm25_true +
  10 * spatial_risk + rnorm(N, 0, 10)
expected <- (cvd_rate / 100000) * population * 5
observed <- rpois(N, expected)
smr      <- observed / pmax(expected, 1)

pts$lon <- lon
pts$lat <- lat
pts$x   <- xy[, 1]
pts$y   <- xy[, 2]
pts$pm25_true   <- pm25_true
pts$pm25        <- pm25
pts$pct_poverty <- pct_poverty
pts$population  <- population
pts$spatial_risk <- spatial_risk
pts$cvd_rate    <- cvd_rate
pts$observed    <- observed
pts$expected    <- expected
pts$smr         <- smr

df <- st_drop_geometry(pts)
write_csv(df, file.path(out_dir, "point_sim.csv"))

cat(sprintf(
  "N=%d points | PM2.5 field mean=%.1f | measured mean=%.1f SD=%.1f (range %.1f–%.1f) | CVD=%.1f/100k\n",
  N, mean(pm25_true), mean(pm25), sd(pm25), min(pm25), max(pm25), mean(cvd_rate)
))

N=1000 points | PM2.5 field mean=9.5 | measured mean=9.4 SD=2.7 (range 3.0–17.6) | CVD=201.2/100k

cat(sprintf(
  "states sampled=%d | pop median=%s | observed deaths total=%s\n",
  n_distinct(pts$state), format(median(population), big.mark = ","),
  format(sum(observed), big.mark = ",")
))

states sampled=47 | pop median=34,230.5 | observed deaths total=594,171



# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Exposure-response: true field vs measured (regression dilution)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
slope <- function(...) {
  X <- cbind(1, ...)
  unname(coef(lm.fit(X, cvd_rate))[2])
}

cat(sprintf("True PM2.5 effect                     = %.2f\n", TRUE_PM25))

True PM2.5 effect                     = 2.50

cat(sprintf(
  "Naive, MEASURED (pm25 only)           = %.2f   <- + confounding\n",
  slope(pm25)
))

Naive, MEASURED (pm25 only)           = 1.91   <- + confounding

cat(sprintf(
  "Adjusted, TRUE field  (+pov +spatial) = %.2f\n",
  slope(pm25_true, pct_poverty, spatial_risk)
))

Adjusted, TRUE field  (+pov +spatial) = 2.51

cat(sprintf(
  "Adjusted, MEASURED    (+pov +spatial) = %.2f   <- attenuated by the nugget\n",
  slope(pm25, pct_poverty, spatial_risk)
))

Adjusted, MEASURED    (+pov +spatial) = 1.83   <- attenuated by the nugget


The naive regression of CVD on measured PM2.5 is biased by the unmeasured spatial confounder. Adjusting for poverty and the spatial-risk field recovers the true coefficient when the latent field is used, but the same adjustment on measured PM2.5 is attenuated by the nugget — classical measurement-error (regression dilution) bias.

title: Environmental Epidemiology
section: 2. Empirical semivariogram of detrended PM2.5 (recover the injected range)
text:
2. Empirical semivariogram of detrended PM2.5 (recover the injected range)
The empirical semivariogram is a key tool in geostatistics to summarise how similar or dissimilar measurements are as a function of distance, capturing spatial correlation structure in a dataset.
Here, we use the empirical semivariogram to quantify spatial structure in the detrended PM2.5 field — that is, the PM2.5 data with large-scale geographic trends (longitude/latitude) removed. Detrending focuses on the spatial “nugget” and range instead of broad trends.
This method helps us check if our simulated PM2.5 data (with its built-in spatial correlation/range) can have its effective range visually recovered from the observed data using only spatial patterns in the residuals.
The steps include: 1. Fit and remove a trend (regression on longitude/latitude) from the PM2.5 point data. 2. Compute the differences between all pairs of residuals and square them (or use gstat::variogram). 3. Group the squared differences into distance bins — the mean of each bin provides the empirical semivariance (γ) at that distance. 4. Plot semivariance against distance, which typically increases then plateaus; the “range” is the distance where this flattening occurs, revealing up to what scale points are spatially correlated.
In this notebook, you will see a semivariogram plot showing how PM2.5 residual similarity decays with geographic distance, and a vertical dashed line indicating the effective range that was injected into the simulation. This visualisation confirms if the simulated spatial range is recovered empirically.

# Detrend measured PM2.5 on lon/lat, then empirical semivariogram via gstat
pts$resid <- residuals(lm(pm25 ~ lon + lat, data = pts))

v_emp <- variogram(resid ~ 1, pts, cutoff = 1.2e6, width = 8e4)

states <- county_shapes %>%
  group_by(STATE) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop")

p_pm <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, aes(colour = pm25), size = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "µg/m³") +
  labs(title = sprintf("Measured PM2.5 at %d sample points", N)) +
  theme_map()

p_cvd <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, aes(colour = cvd_rate), size = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "/100k", option = "magma") +
  labs(title = "Simulated CVD rate at sample points") +
  theme_map()

p_vg <- ggplot(v_emp, aes(dist / 1000, gamma)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "#2b6cb0") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2b6cb0") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3 * RANGE_PM, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 3 * RANGE_PM + 20, y = min(v_emp$gamma, na.rm = TRUE),
    label = sprintf("eff. range ≈ %.0f km", 3 * RANGE_PM),
    hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Distance (km)", y = "Semivariance γ(h)",
    title = "Semivariogram — detrended PM2.5"
  ) +
  expand_limits(y = 0)

p_maps <- (p_pm | p_cvd | p_vg) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Point-referenced PM2.5 field, CVD, and empirical semivariogram")
print(p_maps)







ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "point_maps.png"), p_maps,
       width = 18, height = 5, dpi = 130)

title: Environmental Epidemiology
section: 3. Exposure Assessment: Interpolating Point Data to Areas
text:
3. Exposure Assessment: Interpolating Point Data to Areas
Air quality monitors are located at specific points but we need estimates at every sample location (and, in applied work, at county centroids or census tracts).
Methods: | Method | Principle | Smoothness | Use case | |——–|———–|————|———-| | IDW | Weight = 1/distance^p | Moderate | Quick, no model | | Kriging (ordinary) | Geostatistical, uses variogram | Smooth | Optimal linear prediction | | Nearest monitor | Assign to closest monitor | Abrupt | Worst but common | | Land-use regression | Predict from land use covariates | Flexible | Urban studies |
We place 35 monitors on US land. Each monitor reads the latent PM2.5 field (inverse-distance from nearby sample points) plus instrument error, then we interpolate back to all sample locations and compare against the true field.

idw_knn <- function(query_xy, source_xy, values, p = 2, k = 8) {
  k <- min(k, nrow(source_xy))
  nq <- nrow(query_xy)
  out <- numeric(nq)
  for (i in seq_len(nq)) {
    d <- sqrt((source_xy[, 1] - query_xy[i, 1])^2 +
                (source_xy[, 2] - query_xy[i, 2])^2)
    idx <- order(d)[seq_len(k)]
    w <- 1 / (d[idx] + 1e-10)^p
    out[i] <- sum((w / sum(w)) * values[idx])
  }
  out
}

set.seed(13)
N_MONITORS <- 35
mon_pick <- sample.int(nrow(county_shapes), N_MONITORS, replace = TRUE,
                       prob = pmax(as.numeric(st_area(county_shapes)), 1))
mon_geoms <- lapply(mon_pick, function(i) place_in_poly(county_shapes$geometry[i]))
mon <- st_sf(
  tibble(mon_id = seq_len(N_MONITORS)),
  geometry = st_sfc(mon_geoms, crs = st_crs(county_shapes))
)
mon_xy <- st_coordinates(mon)

# Monitors sample the true field (IDW from point support) + instrument error
mon$pm25 <- pmin(pmax(
  idw_knn(mon_xy, xy, pm25_true, p = 2, k = 6) + rnorm(N_MONITORS, 0, 1),
  3), 28)

# Nearest monitor
nn <- st_nearest_feature(pts, mon)
pts$pm25_nearest <- mon$pm25[nn]

# IDW (gstat, p = 2, k = 10)
idw_pred <- gstat::idw(
  pm25 ~ 1, locations = mon, newdata = pts,
  idp = 2, nmax = 10, debug.level = 0
)
pts$pm25_idw <- idw_pred$var1.pred

# Ordinary kriging with exponential model matching the injected range
# (gstat Exp: C(h) = psill * exp(-h/a); a in metres)
vgm_ok <- vgm(psill = PSILL_PM, model = "Exp",
              range = RANGE_PM * 1000, nugget = NUGGET_SD^2)
ok_pred <- krige(
  pm25 ~ 1, mon, newdata = pts, model = vgm_ok,
  debug.level = 0
)
pts$pm25_krige <- pmin(pmax(ok_pred$var1.pred, 3), 30)

df <- st_drop_geometry(pts)

interp_cols <- c(
  pm25_true    = "True PM2.5 field",
  pm25_nearest = "Nearest monitor",
  pm25_idw     = "IDW (p=2, k=10)",
  pm25_krige   = "Ordinary kriging (Exp)"
)
vmin <- as.numeric(quantile(df$pm25_true, 0.05))
vmax <- as.numeric(quantile(df$pm25_true, 0.95))

interp_plot <- function(col, title) {
  r <- cor(df$pm25_true, df[[col]])
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = states, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_sf(data = pts, aes(colour = .data[[col]]), size = 0.7) +
    geom_sf(data = mon, shape = 17, size = 2.2, colour = "#1D4ED8") +
    scale_colour_distiller(
      name = "PM2.5", palette = "YlOrBr", direction = 1,
      limits = c(vmin, vmax), oob = scales::squish
    ) +
    labs(title = sprintf("%s (r=%.3f with truth)", title, r)) +
    theme_map()
}

p_interp <- (
  interp_plot("pm25_true",    interp_cols[["pm25_true"]]) |
    interp_plot("pm25_nearest", interp_cols[["pm25_nearest"]])
) / (
  interp_plot("pm25_idw",     interp_cols[["pm25_idw"]]) |
    interp_plot("pm25_krige",   interp_cols[["pm25_krige"]])
) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "PM2.5 exposure assessment: interpolation methods (monitors sample the true field)"
  )
print(p_interp)







ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "pm25_interpolation.png"), p_interp,
       width = 14, height = 9, dpi = 130)

for (col in c("pm25_nearest", "pm25_idw", "pm25_krige")) {
  r <- cor(df$pm25_true, df[[col]])
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((df$pm25_true - df[[col]])^2))
  cat(sprintf("%-14s r(vs true field)=%.3f  RMSE=%.2f\n", col, r, rmse))
}

pm25_nearest   r(vs true field)=0.440  RMSE=2.62
pm25_idw       r(vs true field)=0.542  RMSE=2.11
pm25_krige     r(vs true field)=0.569  RMSE=1.90


Nearest-neighbour assignment is piecewise constant and typically has the highest RMSE. IDW is a fast, parameter-light smoother. Ordinary kriging uses the variogram (here, the exponential model that generated the field) and is the best linear unbiased predictor under that model — provided the variogram is well specified.

title: Environmental Epidemiology
text:
4. Exposure-Response Analysis: Ecological Regression
Ecological regression is a way to study relationships between group-level variables — like average air pollution and disease rates.
Imagine you want to see if more polluted places have higher disease rates. For each sample location (standing in for a community), you have: - the average PM2.5 air pollution value - the rate of cardiovascular disease (CVD)
We fit a (linear) model:
CVD_rate = a + b × PM2.5 + c × poverty + random_noise

CVD_rate: Disease rate at the location
a: The “baseline” rate if pollution and poverty are 0
b: How much the disease rate goes up for each step in PM2.5 (the main thing we care about)
c: How much poverty affects disease rate

The model tries to find b — the change in CVD rate for each additional µg/m³ of PM2.5 — by drawing a line that best fits all location-level data points.
In plain English: we’re seeing whether more polluted places have more heart disease, after accounting for poverty.

# Ecological regression: CVD rate ~ measured PM2.5 + poverty
model_eco <- lm(cvd_rate ~ pm25 + pct_poverty, data = df)
print(summary(model_eco)$coefficients)

              Estimate Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 150.932609  4.9367506 30.573270 2.319920e-145
pm25          1.937337  0.1688945 11.470698  1.068263e-28
pct_poverty   2.189487  0.3160622  6.927395  7.678054e-12

pm25_coef <- coef(model_eco)[["pm25"]]
cat(sprintf("\nTrue PM2.5 coefficient: %.1f CVD deaths/100k per µg/m³\n", TRUE_PM25))


True PM2.5 coefficient: 2.5 CVD deaths/100k per µg/m³

cat(sprintf("Estimated coefficient : %.1f\n", pm25_coef))

Estimated coefficient : 1.9

cat(sprintf("Bias                  : %+.2f\n", pm25_coef - TRUE_PM25))

Bias                  : -0.56

x_line <- seq(min(df$pm25), max(df$pm25), length.out = 100)
y_pred <- (coef(model_eco)[["(Intercept)"]] +
             coef(model_eco)[["pm25"]] * x_line +
             coef(model_eco)[["pct_poverty"]] * mean(df$pct_poverty))

p_er <- ggplot(df, aes(pm25, cvd_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1, colour = "#4878CF") +
  geom_line(data = tibble(pm25 = x_line, cvd_rate = y_pred),
            colour = "#DC2626", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Measured PM2.5 (µg/m³)",
    y = "CVD rate per 100k",
    title = "Exposure-response: PM2.5 → CVD mortality",
    subtitle = sprintf("β = %.2f (true: %.1f)", pm25_coef, TRUE_PM25)
  )

coef_by_method <- tibble(
  method = c("Nearest", "IDW", "Kriging"),
  col    = c("pm25_nearest", "pm25_idw", "pm25_krige")
) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    beta = coef(lm(df$cvd_rate ~ df[[col]] + df$pct_poverty))[2]
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

p_bar <- ggplot(coef_by_method, aes(method, beta, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = TRUE_PM25, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Nearest = "#D65F5F", IDW = "#4878CF", Kriging = "#6ACC65")) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "PM2.5 coefficient",
    title = "Coefficient by exposure method",
    subtitle = "Exposure measurement error matters"
  )

p_eco <- p_er | p_bar
print(p_eco)







ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "exposure_response.png"), p_eco,
       width = 14, height = 5, dpi = 130)

title: Environmental Epidemiology
text:
5. Environmental Justice Analysis
Environmental justice (EJ) analysis asks: are pollution and other environmental risks shared equally among all groups, or do some (often already disadvantaged) groups bear a greater burden?
In this section, we look at whether PM2.5 exposure is higher in communities with more poverty (and, as a simulated demographic, higher minority share). This helps highlight possible inequities in who is most affected by pollution. We compare pollution levels across poverty tertiles, map the burden, and compute disparity ratios.

set.seed(42)
df$pct_minority   <- pmin(pmax(20 + 15 * rbeta(N, 2, 3), 0), 100)
df$pct_low_income <- pmin(pmax(df$pct_poverty * 2.5 + rnorm(N, 0, 5), 0), 100)
df$poverty_tertile <- factor(
  ntile(df$pct_poverty, 3),
  labels = c("Low poverty", "Middle", "High poverty")
)
pts$poverty_tertile <- df$poverty_tertile
pts$pct_minority    <- df$pct_minority

ej <- df %>%
  group_by(poverty_tertile) %>%
  summarise(mean_pm25 = mean(pm25), .groups = "drop")

ratio_hl <- ej$mean_pm25[ej$poverty_tertile == "High poverty"] /
  ej$mean_pm25[ej$poverty_tertile == "Low poverty"]

p_ej_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, aes(colour = pm25), size = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_distiller(name = "PM2.5", palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1) +
  labs(title = "PM2.5 at sample points") +
  theme_map()

p_box <- ggplot(df, aes(poverty_tertile, pm25, fill = poverty_tertile)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#A1D99B", "#FEC44F", "#D95F0E")) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)",
    title = "PM2.5 by poverty tertile",
    subtitle = sprintf("High/low disparity ratio = %.2fx", ratio_hl)
  )

p_bar_ej <- ggplot(ej, aes(poverty_tertile, mean_pm25, fill = poverty_tertile)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white", width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#A1D99B", "#FEC44F", "#D95F0E")) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean PM2.5 (µg/m³)", title = "Mean PM2.5 by poverty tertile")

p_min <- ggplot(df, aes(pct_minority, pm25, colour = pct_poverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_distiller(name = "% poverty", palette = "RdYlGn", direction = -1) +
  labs(
    x = "% minority (simulated)", y = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)",
    title = sprintf(
      "Minority share vs PM2.5 (r = %.3f)",
      cor(df$pct_minority, df$pm25)
    )
  )

p_ej <- (p_ej_map | p_box) / (p_bar_ej | p_min) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Environmental justice analysis: disparities in pollution exposure")
print(p_ej)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "ej_analysis.png"), p_ej,
       width = 14, height = 10, dpi = 130)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

cat("Environmental justice summary:\n")

Environmental justice summary:

cat(sprintf("  Correlation: minority%% vs PM2.5 = %.3f\n", cor(df$pct_minority, df$pm25)))

  Correlation: minority% vs PM2.5 = -0.080

cat(sprintf("  High-poverty tertile PM2.5  : %.1f µg/m³\n",
            ej$mean_pm25[ej$poverty_tertile == "High poverty"]))

  High-poverty tertile PM2.5  : 9.4 µg/m³

cat(sprintf("  Low-poverty tertile PM2.5   : %.1f µg/m³\n",
            ej$mean_pm25[ej$poverty_tertile == "Low poverty"]))

  Low-poverty tertile PM2.5   : 9.6 µg/m³

cat(sprintf("  Inequality ratio (high/low) : %.2fx\n", ratio_hl))

  Inequality ratio (high/low) : 0.97x


A disparity ratio above 1 means the highest-poverty tertile bears a heavier pollution burden. In real EJ screening (e.g. EPA EJScreen, CalEnviroScreen), this kind of overlay of environmental hazard and socioeconomic vulnerability is the starting point — not a causal claim.

title: Environmental Epidemiology
section: 6. Ecological Fallacy: Individual vs Aggregate Data
text:
6. Ecological Fallacy: Individual vs Aggregate Data
Imagine you want to know if breathing more air pollution (like PM2.5) makes individuals more likely to get heart disease. If you only look at the average air pollution and the average heart disease rates for each community (big groups), you might see a pattern. But this does not always mean that the same trend is true for each person.
The ecological fallacy happens when you take results from group-level data (like counties or cities) and assume they must be true for individuals within those groups. This is risky because group averages can hide what is really happening among individuals. Other factors can mix things up (like richer counties may have less pollution and better healthcare, but within each county, poor people may still be the most at risk).
Key takeaway: just because there is a pattern between pollution and disease at the county level, does not guarantee you will see it (or the same strength) for individual people. Be careful when jumping from group data to conclusions about individuals.

set.seed(7)
N_IND <- 10000

# Individual PM2.5 (based on assigned location + within-area variation)
ind_loc      <- sample.int(N, N_IND, replace = TRUE)
ind_pm25     <- df$pm25[ind_loc] + rnorm(N_IND, 0, 3)
ind_poverty  <- df$pct_poverty[ind_loc] + rnorm(N_IND, 0, 5)
ind_age      <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(N_IND, 55, 15), 20), 90)

TRUE_IND_PM25 <- 0.015   # log-OR per µg/m³ at individual level
ind_logit <- -3.5 + TRUE_IND_PM25 * ind_pm25 + 0.02 * (ind_age - 55) +
  0.015 * (ind_poverty - 10) + rnorm(N_IND, 0, 0.5)
ind_cvd <- rbinom(N_IND, 1, 1 / (1 + exp(-ind_logit)))

eco_coef_log_rr <- coef(lm(log(cvd_rate) ~ pm25, data = df))[["pm25"]]
ind_fit <- glm(ind_cvd ~ ind_pm25 + ind_age + ind_poverty, family = binomial())
ind_coef_log_or <- coef(ind_fit)[["ind_pm25"]]

cat("Ecological fallacy demonstration:\n")

Ecological fallacy demonstration:

cat(sprintf("  True individual log-OR per µg/m³ PM2.5: %.4f\n", TRUE_IND_PM25))

  True individual log-OR per µg/m³ PM2.5: 0.0150

cat(sprintf("  Individual-level logistic estimate     : %.4f\n", ind_coef_log_or))

  Individual-level logistic estimate     : 0.0345

cat(sprintf("  Location-level ecological estimate     : %.4f\n", eco_coef_log_rr))

  Location-level ecological estimate     : 0.0095

cat("\nThe ecological and individual-level estimates are on different scales\n")


The ecological and individual-level estimates are on different scales

cat("(rate ratio vs odds ratio) and answer different questions.\n")

(rate ratio vs odds ratio) and answer different questions.

cat("DO NOT use group-level coefficients to make individual-level inferences!\n")

DO NOT use group-level coefficients to make individual-level inferences!

text:
7. Knowledge Check

IDW gives PM2.5 coefficient β = 2.1 while kriging gives β = 2.8. Which should you prefer and why?
PM2.5 exposure and poverty are correlated (r = 0.41). How does this affect the ecological regression for PM2.5’s health effect?
The EJ analysis shows the highest-poverty tertile has 1.4× higher PM2.5 than the lowest. Is this statistically significant? How would you test it?
Individual-level PM2.5 log-OR = 0.015 vs ecological log-RR = 0.07. Why do these differ? What is the ecological fallacy specifically?
Implement Moran’s I for PM2.5 exposure to quantify spatial patterning of the exposure surface.


# Exercise 5 — distance-band Moran's I for measured PM2.5 (no spdep)
band_km <- 200
w <- 1 / Dkm
diag(w) <- 0
w[Dkm > band_km] <- 0
rs <- rowSums(w)
w[rs > 0, ] <- w[rs > 0, ] / rs[rs > 0]

z <- as.numeric(scale(df$pm25, scale = TRUE, center = TRUE))
n_w <- sum(w)
moran_i <- as.numeric((N / n_w) * (t(z) %*% w %*% z) / sum(z^2))
cat(sprintf(
  "Moran's I for measured PM2.5 (%.0f km distance band): %.3f\n",
  band_km, moran_i
))

Moran's I for measured PM2.5 (200 km distance band): 0.419

cat("I > 0 indicates positive spatial autocorrelation (clustered exposure).\n")

title: Disease Mapping & Bayesian Smoothing
text:
2. The Small-Area Estimation
Small-Area Estimation (SAE) refers to statistical methods used to produce reliable estimates of quantities (such as disease rates) for small geographic areas or population subgroups, where direct survey data is sparse or highly variable. Instead of relying only on local data — which may be noisy or unreliable for small places — SAE combines information from similar areas, related predictors, or statistical models to “borrow strength.” This helps stabilise estimates, reduce random error, and provide more trustworthy results, especially in regions with limited data. In public health, SAE is crucial for mapping disease rates in all counties or neighbourhoods, not just places with large populations or many survey respondents.

2.1 The Small-Area Estimation Problem
Imagine you run a national health survey and someone asks you for the diabetes rate in every county. The catch: a survey designed for national numbers might only catch six people in some small rural county. A rate computed from six people is basically noise — one unlucky draw reads 0%, another reads 33%. That “just use whoever you sampled there” number is called the direct estimate, and in small areas it’s too wobbly to trust. Small Area Estimation (SAE) is the set of tricks for getting believable numbers for those little areas anyway.
The core move: borrowing strength. Instead of trusting those six people alone, SAE blends them with information from outside the county. It borrows from two places:

Predictors that exist everywhere. Obesity, age structure, poverty, food access come from the census and administrative records for every county — no survey needed. If you know how those track with diabetes (a regression), you can predict a county’s rate even where you sampled almost nobody.
Neighbouring or similar areas. Nearby counties carry information about each other, so you let them lend each other statistical weight (spatial smoothing).

Usually you use both.
The mechanism: shrinkage. The final estimate is a weighted average of the noisy local direct estimate and the model’s prediction — and the weighting is the clever bit, because it adapts to how much local data you have. Big sample in a county → trust the direct number, barely nudge it. Tiny sample → lean hard on the model. Estimates get “shrunk” toward the model prediction by an amount proportional to how unreliable they are. You trade a little bias for a big cut in variance, and on average land much closer to the truth.
The everyday analogy is rating a restaurant from only three reviews: you don’t take those three at face value, you nudge them toward what you’d expect from similar restaurants nearby — and the fewer reviews there are, the more you rely on that expectation.
Names you’ll bump into. When you only have the aggregated estimate per area plus area-level covariates, the classic tool is the Fay–Herriot area-level model. When you have individual respondent records plus covariates, it’s the Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model. Bolt on spatial or random effects (often estimated in a Bayesian / INLA framework) and you’re in modern SAE.
Where you’ve already met it. The county diabetes prevalence you’ve been running GWR on is almost certainly an SAE product — CDC’s diabetes surveillance and the PLACES project publish county estimates built with model-based small area estimation, precisely because no survey measures every county directly. So your local-regression work sits one layer on top of SAE output.
The catch. All of this leans on the model being reasonable. If the model is wrong, or a county is genuinely unusual in a way the covariates don’t capture, SAE will cheerfully smooth that real signal away — the precision you gained was borrowed against an assumption. That tension between design-based (trust the sample) and model-based (trust the model) thinking is basically the whole craft of the field.
Problem: Observed SMR = \(O_i / E_i\) is unstable for areas with small populations.
A county with expected deaths \(E=2\) and observed \(O=4\) has SMR=2.0, suggesting 100% excess mortality — but this could easily be random variation.
Key insight: Raw rates have high variance in low-population areas. Bayesian methods “borrow strength” from neighbouring areas and the overall mean.



Method
