5. The 10% Change Rule for Confounding

cat("Systematic 10% change rule across all predictors\n\n")

Systematic 10% change rule across all predictors

cat(sprintf("%-20s %10s %10s %10s %12s\n",
            "Predictor", "Crude OR", "Adj OR", "% Change", "Confounder?"))

Predictor              Crude OR     Adj OR   % Change  Confounder?

cat(paste(rep("-", 65), collapse = ""), "\n")

----------------------------------------------------------------- 

outcome_col <- "readmitted"
for (pair in list(
  c("diabetes", "Diabetes"),
  c("hf", "Heart failure"),
  c("age_std", "Age (std)")
)) {
  exposure <- pair[[1]]; label <- pair[[2]]
  # Crude
  if (exposure == "age_std") {
    m_crude <- glm(as.formula(paste(outcome_col, "~", exposure)), data = df, family = binomial())
    cr <- exp(coef(m_crude)[[exposure]])
  } else {
    a <- sum(df[[exposure]] == 1 & df[[outcome_col]] == 1)
    b <- sum(df[[exposure]] == 1 & df[[outcome_col]] == 0)
    c <- sum(df[[exposure]] == 0 & df[[outcome_col]] == 1)
    d <- sum(df[[exposure]] == 0 & df[[outcome_col]] == 0)
    cr <- if (b * c > 0) (a * d) / (b * c) else NA_real_
  }

  # Adjusted (controlling for the other two)
  covariates <- setdiff(c("diabetes", "hf", "age_std"), exposure)
  formula_a  <- as.formula(paste(outcome_col, "~", exposure, "+", paste(covariates, collapse = " + ")))
  m_adj <- glm(formula_a, data = df, family = binomial())
  adj   <- exp(coef(m_adj)[[exposure]])

  pct <- (adj - cr) / cr * 100
  is_conf <- if (abs(pct) > 10) "✗ Yes (>10%)" else "✓ No (<10%)"
  cat(sprintf("%-20s %10.3f %10.3f %+9.1f%% %12s\n", label, cr, adj, pct, is_conf))
}

Diabetes                  1.894      1.723      -9.0% ✓ No (<10%)
Heart failure             2.120      1.920      -9.4% ✓ No (<10%)
Age (std)                 1.082      1.061      -2.0% ✓ No (<10%)

title: Confounding & Effect Modification
text:
6. E-Value: Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding

e_value <- function(RR) {
  # E-value: minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need
  # to fully explain an observed RR, on both the exposure-confounder and
  # confounder-outcome pathways.
  # VanderWeele & Ding (2017) formula.
  if (RR < 1) RR <- 1 / RR   # flip if protective
  RR + sqrt(RR * (RR - 1))
}

# Convert OR to approximate RR using prevalence correction
outcome_prev <- mean(df$readmitted)
or_to_rr <- function(OR, prev) {
  # Zhang & Yu (1998) approximation.
  OR / ((1 - prev) + prev * OR)
}

cat("E-value analysis — sensitivity to unmeasured confounding\n")

E-value analysis — sensitivity to unmeasured confounding

cat(paste(rep("=", 65), collapse = ""), "\n")

================================================================= 

hf_or <- exp(coef(model_adj)[["hf"]])
for (pair in list(
  list("Diabetes → readmission (adj OR)", adj_or_val),
  list("HF → readmission", hf_or)
)) {
  label <- pair[[1]]; OR_val <- pair[[2]]
  RR_approx <- or_to_rr(OR_val, outcome_prev)
  ev <- e_value(RR_approx)
  ev_ci <- e_value(max(1.0, RR_approx / exp(1.96 * 0.15)))  # rough CI lower
  cat(sprintf("\n%s\n", label))
  cat(sprintf("  Adjusted OR ≈ RR  : %.3f\n", RR_approx))
  cat(sprintf("  E-value (point)   : %.2f\n", ev))
  cat(sprintf("  E-value (CI lower): %.2f\n", ev_ci))
  cat("  → An unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with BOTH\n")
  cat(sprintf("    exposure AND outcome by a factor of at least %.1f× to explain away\n", ev))
  cat("    the observed association entirely.\n")
  if (ev > 2.0) {
    cat("  → E-value > 2 suggests robustness to weak confounding.\n")
  } else {
    cat("  → E-value ≤ 2 — association could be explained by a moderate confounder.\n")
  }
}

copd         <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.5 * b[, 3] - 1.0))

obesity      <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.5 * b[, 1] - 0.8))

section: 2. Why Temporal Splits Matter in Healthcare
text:
2. Why Temporal Splits Matter in Healthcare
Random splitting of clinical data leaks future information into training when: - The same patient appears multiple times (train on visit 1, test on visit 2 of the same patient) - Care patterns change over time (COVID, policy changes, new guidelines) - Models evaluated on temporal holdouts reflect real-world deployment performance








Split type
Use when
Risk




Random stratified
Cross-sectional data, no time structure
Data leakage if temporal trends exist


Temporal (chronological)
Time-ordered admissions, EHR data
Better reflects deployment conditions


Patient-level
Same patient across visits
Prevents same-patient leakage


Geographic
Multi-site data
Tests transportability

# Strategy comparison — SMOTE-style interpolation, under-sampling, SMOTE+Tomek
smote_resample <- function(x, y, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  pos <- which(y == 1); neg <- which(y == 0)
  n_need <- length(neg) - length(pos)
  if (n_need <= 0) return(list(x = x, y = y))
  xp <- x[pos, , drop = FALSE]
  i1 <- sample(nrow(xp), n_need, replace = TRUE)
  i2 <- sample(nrow(xp), n_need, replace = TRUE)
  lam <- runif(n_need)
  syn <- xp[i1, , drop = FALSE] * lam + xp[i2, , drop = FALSE] * (1 - lam)
  list(x = rbind(x, syn), y = c(y, rep(1L, n_need)))
}
under_resample <- function(x, y, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  pos <- which(y == 1); neg <- which(y == 0)
  n <- min(length(pos), length(neg))
  idx <- c(sample(pos, n), sample(neg, n))
  list(x = x[idx, , drop = FALSE], y = y[idx])
}
tomek_clean <- function(x, y) {
  # Drop majority points whose nearest neighbour is minority (Tomek-style)
  d <- as.matrix(dist(x))
  diag(d) <- Inf
  nn <- apply(d, 1, which.min)
  drop <- which(y == 0 & y[nn] == 1)
  keep <- setdiff(seq_along(y), drop)
  list(x = x[keep, , drop = FALSE], y = y[keep])
}

6. Cross-Validation Strategies

# Compare stratified k-fold vs time-series CV on the training set
cv_auc_fold <- function(x, y, tr_idx, te_idx) {
  dtr <- as_tibble(x[tr_idx, , drop = FALSE]) %>% mutate(y = y[tr_idx])
  dte <- as_tibble(x[te_idx, , drop = FALSE])
  w   <- ifelse(y[tr_idx] == 1, 0.5 / mean(y[tr_idx] == 1),
                0.5 / mean(y[tr_idx] == 0))
  fit <- glm(y ~ ., data = dtr, family = binomial, weights = w)
  auc_prob(y[te_idx], predict(fit, newdata = dte, type = "response"))
}

# Stratified k-fold (appropriate for cross-sectional data)
set.seed(42)
train_cv <- as_tibble(X_train_pp) %>% mutate(y = factor(y_train, levels = c(0, 1)))
skf <- vfold_cv(train_cv, v = 5, strata = y)
cv_skf <- map_dbl(skf$splits, function(sp) {
  cv_auc_fold(X_train_pp, y_train, as.integer(sp$in_id),
              setdiff(seq_len(nrow(train_cv)), as.integer(sp$in_id)))
})

  tr_idx <- seq_len(train_end)
  te_idx <- (train_end + 1):min(test_end, n)

})

1. Setup & Dataset

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(xgboost)
library(lightgbm)
library(ranger)
library(patchwork)
tidymodels_prefer()
set.seed(42)

mod04_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mod04")
dir.create(mod04_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
)
col_blue <- "#2563EB"; col_red <- "#DC2626"; col_green <- "#16A34A"
col_purple <- "#7C3AED"; col_navy <- "#1E3A8A"

auc_prob   <- function(y, p) yardstick::roc_auc_vec(factor(y, levels = c(0, 1)), p, event_level = "second")
ap_prob    <- function(y, p) yardstick::pr_auc_vec(factor(y, levels = c(0, 1)), p, event_level = "second")
brier_prob <- function(y, p) mean((p - y)^2)

cat(sprintf("XGBoost %s\n", as.character(packageVersion("xgboost"))))

XGBoost 3.2.1.1

cat(sprintf("LightGBM %s\n", as.character(packageVersion("lightgbm"))))

LightGBM 4.7.0

# ── Dataset ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
set.seed(42); N <- 3000
sig <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
clip <- function(x, lo, hi) pmin(pmax(x, lo), hi)
b <- matrix(rnorm(N * 4), ncol = 4); set.seed(99)
age <- as.integer(clip(rnorm(N, 62, 15), 18, 92))
sex <- sample(c("M", "F"), N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.48, 0.52))
payer <- sample(c("Medicare", "Medicaid", "Private", "Self-pay", "Other"),
                N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.40, 0.22, 0.28, 0.07, 0.03))
admit_type <- sample(c("Emergency", "Elective", "Urgent"),
                     N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.52, 0.30, 0.18))
los_days <- as.integer(clip(round(rgamma(N, shape = 2.5, scale = 1.8)), 1, 30))
diabetes <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.6 * b[, 1] - 0.5 + 0.02 * (age - 62) / 15))
hypertension <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.7 * b[, 1] - 0.2))
hf <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.4 * b[, 2] + 0.5 * hypertension - 1.5))
copd <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.5 * b[, 3] - 1.0))
ckd <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.5 * b[, 1] + 0.6 * diabetes - 1.2))
obesity <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.5 * b[, 1] - 0.8))
depression <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(0.3 * b[, 4] - 1.4))
n_comorb <- diabetes + hypertension + hf + copd + ckd
set.seed(21)
glucose <- round(clip(rnorm(N, 105 + 15 * diabetes, 28), 50, 400), 1)
creatinine <- round(clip(rgamma(N, shape = 1.6 + 0.8 * hf, scale = 0.6), 0.4, 10), 2)
hba1c <- round(clip(rnorm(N, 6.5 + 0.8 * diabetes, 1.4), 4, 14), 1)
sbp <- round(clip(rnorm(N, 128 + 12 * hypertension, 18), 80, 200), 0)
bmi <- round(clip(rnorm(N, 28 + 4 * obesity, 6), 15, 55), 1)
logit <- (-3.2 + 0.6 * hf + 0.5 * diabetes + 0.5 * ckd + 0.3 * copd +
            0.02 * (age - 62) / 15 +
            0.3 * as.integer(admit_type == "Emergency") +
            0.25 * as.integer(payer == "Medicaid") +
            0.2 * as.integer(los_days > 7) +
            0.5 * hf * diabetes + rnorm(N, 0, 0.25))
readmitted <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(logit))
df <- tibble(
  age, sex, payer, admit_type, los_days,
  diabetes, hypertension, hf, copd, ckd, obesity, depression, n_comorb,
  glucose, creatinine, hba1c, sbp, bmi, readmitted
)
df$los_gt7 <- as.integer(df$los_days > 7)
NUMERIC <- c("age", "los_days", "n_comorb", "glucose", "creatinine", "hba1c", "sbp", "bmi")
BINARY <- c("diabetes", "hypertension", "hf", "copd", "ckd", "obesity", "depression", "los_gt7")
CATEGORIC <- c("sex", "payer", "admit_type")
FEATURES <- c(NUMERIC, BINARY, CATEGORIC); TARGET <- "readmitted"

set.seed(42)
df_ml <- df %>%
  select(all_of(c(FEATURES, TARGET))) %>%
  mutate(readmitted = factor(readmitted, levels = c(0, 1)))
split_te <- initial_split(df_ml, prop = 0.80, strata = readmitted)
df_tr_all <- training(split_te); df_te <- testing(split_te)
split_val <- initial_split(df_tr_all, prop = 0.85, strata = readmitted)
df_tr2 <- training(split_val); df_val <- testing(split_val)

rec <- recipe(readmitted ~ ., data = df_tr2) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_of(NUMERIC)) %>%
  step_normalize(all_of(NUMERIC)) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_of(BINARY)) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_of(CATEGORIC)) %>%
  step_dummy(all_of(CATEGORIC), one_hot = TRUE)
rec_prep <- prep(rec, training = df_tr2)
bake_x <- function(newdata) bake(rec_prep, new_data = newdata) %>% select(-readmitted)
Xtr_tbl  <- bake_x(df_tr2); Xval_tbl <- bake_x(df_val); Xte_tbl <- bake_x(df_te)
Xtr  <- as.matrix(Xtr_tbl);  Xval <- as.matrix(Xval_tbl); Xte <- as.matrix(Xte_tbl)
y_tr2 <- as.integer(as.character(df_tr2$readmitted))
y_val  <- as.integer(as.character(df_val$readmitted))
y_te   <- as.integer(as.character(df_te$readmitted))
feat_nm <- colnames(Xtr)
scale_pos <- sum(y_tr2 == 0) / sum(y_tr2 == 1)
cat(sprintf("Train:%s | Val:%s | Test:%s\n",
            paste(dim(Xtr), collapse = " x "),
            paste(dim(Xval), collapse = " x "),
            paste(dim(Xte), collapse = " x ")))

Train:2039 x 26 | Val:360 x 26 | Test:601 x 26

cat(sprintf("scale_pos_weight for XGBoost: %.2f\n", scale_pos))

scale_pos_weight for XGBoost: 8.48

title: XGBoost & LightGBM
text:
2. Gradient Boosting — Conceptual Overview
Iteration 0:  predict mean (F₀)
Iteration 1:  fit a tree to residuals r₁ = y - F₀  →  F₁ = F₀ + η·h₁
Iteration 2:  fit a tree to residuals r₂ = y - F₁  →  F₂ = F₁ + η·h₂
...
Iteration T:  F_T = F₀ + η·Σ hₜ







Concept
Effect




Learning rate η
Shrinks each tree’s contribution — smaller = more trees needed but better generalization


n_estimators
Number of trees — use early stopping to find optimal T


max_depth
Tree depth — shallower = more regularization


subsample / colsample
Stochastic gradient boosting — reduces overfitting


scale_pos_weight
XGBoost class-imbalance correction = N_neg / N_pos




# ── XGBoost with early stopping ───────────────────────────────────────────────
dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(Xtr,  label = y_tr2)
dval   <- xgb.DMatrix(Xval, label = y_val)
dte    <- xgb.DMatrix(Xte,  label = y_te)

xgb_params <- list(
  objective        = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric      = "auc",
  eta              = 0.05,          # learning rate
  max_depth        = 6,
  subsample        = 0.8,
  colsample_bytree = 0.8,
  scale_pos_weight = scale_pos,     # handle class imbalance
  seed             = 42,
  verbosity        = 0
)
xgb_model <- xgb.train(
  params = xgb_params, data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 500,
  evals = list(train = dtrain, val = dval),
  early_stopping_rounds = 30,
  verbose = 0
)
prob_xgb <- predict(xgb_model, dte)
auc_xgb  <- auc_prob(y_te, prob_xgb)
best_iter_xgb <- attr(xgb_model, "early_stop")$best_iteration
if (is.null(best_iter_xgb)) best_iter_xgb <- xgb.get.num.boosted.rounds(xgb_model)
cat(sprintf("XGBoost: best_iteration=%d, AUC=%.4f\n", best_iter_xgb, auc_xgb))

XGBoost: best_iteration=30, AUC=0.6753

# Learning curve
ev <- as_tibble(attr(xgb_model, "evaluation_log"))
p_lc <- ggplot(ev, aes(iter)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = train_auc, colour = "Train AUC"), linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = val_auc,   colour = "Val AUC"),   linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_iter_xgb, colour = col_green, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Train AUC" = col_blue, "Val AUC" = col_red)) +
  labs(x = "Boosting round", y = "AUC", colour = NULL,
       title = "XGBoost learning curve — early stopping",
       subtitle = sprintf("Best iteration = %d", best_iter_xgb))
print(p_lc)







ggsave(file.path(mod04_dir, "xgb_learning_curve.png"), p_lc, width = 10, height = 4, dpi = 120)


# ── LightGBM — faster, handles categoricals natively ─────────────────────────
df_lgb <- df %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(CATEGORIC), as.factor))
X_lgb <- df_lgb %>% select(all_of(c(NUMERIC, BINARY, CATEGORIC)))
y_lgb <- df_lgb[[TARGET]]
set.seed(42)
# Recreate the same 80/20 then 85/15 splits on the categorical-aware frame
lgb_ml <- X_lgb %>% mutate(readmitted = factor(y_lgb, levels = c(0, 1)))
sp_te  <- initial_split(lgb_ml, prop = 0.80, strata = readmitted)
Xl_tr_all <- training(sp_te); Xl_te <- testing(sp_te)
sp_val <- initial_split(Xl_tr_all, prop = 0.85, strata = readmitted)
Xl_tr2 <- training(sp_val); Xl_val <- testing(sp_val)
yl_tr2 <- as.integer(as.character(Xl_tr2$readmitted))
yl_val  <- as.integer(as.character(Xl_val$readmitted))
yl_te   <- as.integer(as.character(Xl_te$readmitted))
Xl_tr2_x <- Xl_tr2 %>% select(-readmitted)
Xl_val_x <- Xl_val %>% select(-readmitted)
Xl_te_x  <- Xl_te  %>% select(-readmitted)

# LightGBM wants integer codes for categoricals
to_lgb_mat <- function(d) {
  d2 <- d
  for (col in CATEGORIC) d2[[col]] <- as.integer(d2[[col]]) - 1L
  as.matrix(d2)
}
cat_idx <- match(CATEGORIC, names(Xl_tr2_x)) - 1L  # 0-based for lightgbm
dtrain_l <- lgb.Dataset(to_lgb_mat(Xl_tr2_x), label = yl_tr2, categorical_feature = cat_idx)
dval_l   <- lgb.Dataset(to_lgb_mat(Xl_val_x),  label = yl_val,  categorical_feature = cat_idx,
                        reference = dtrain_l)

lgb_params <- list(
  objective        = "binary",
  metric           = "auc",
  learning_rate    = 0.05,
  num_leaves       = 31,
  max_depth        = -1,
  subsample        = 0.8,
  colsample_bytree = 0.8,
  is_unbalance     = TRUE,
  verbosity        = -1,
  seed             = 42
)
lgb_model <- lgb.train(
  params = lgb_params, data = dtrain_l,
  nrounds = 500,
  valids = list(train = dtrain_l, val = dval_l),
  early_stopping_rounds = 30,
  verbose = -1
)
prob_lgb <- predict(lgb_model, to_lgb_mat(Xl_te_x))
auc_lgb  <- auc_prob(yl_te, prob_lgb)
cat(sprintf("LightGBM: best_iteration=%d, AUC=%.4f\n", lgb_model$best_iter, auc_lgb))

set.seed(42)

xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(),
  sample_size = tune(), min_n = tune(), mtry = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost", scale_pos_weight = scale_pos) %>%
  set_mode("classification")

bayes_data <- Xtr_tbl %>% mutate(readmitted = factor(y_tr2, levels = c(0, 1)))

  add_model(xgb_spec) %>%

  update(

Random search  :  30 configs | best AUC=0.6897 | time=28.1s

# Successive halving (factor = 3) on the same grid
# Evaluate all configs on a small subsample, keep top 1/3, expand data, repeat
halving_search <- function(grid, data, factor_h = 3, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- nrow(data)
  sizes <- unique(pmin(n, round(n * (factor_h^(0:2)) / (factor_h^2))))
  sizes[length(sizes)] <- n
  remain <- grid
  last_scores <- NULL
  for (s in sizes) {
    idx <- sample.int(n, s)
    sub <- data[idx, ]
    folds_h <- vfold_cv(sub, v = 3, strata = readmitted)
    tun <- tune_grid(
      xgb_wf, resamples = folds_h, grid = remain,
      metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
      control = control_grid(verbose = FALSE)
    )
    ranked <- collect_metrics(tun) %>%
      filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>%
      arrange(desc(mean))
    last_scores <- ranked
    n_keep <- max(1, floor(nrow(ranked) / factor_h))
    keep_cols <- names(remain)
    remain <- ranked %>% select(all_of(keep_cols)) %>% slice_head(n = n_keep)
  }
  last_scores
}
t0 <- Sys.time()
hs <- halving_search(grid, train_baked, factor_h = 3, seed = 42)
t_halv <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))
cat(sprintf("Halving grid   : auto reduce | best AUC=%.4f | time=%.1fs\n",
            hs$mean[1], t_halv))

text:
3. Nested Cross-Validation — Unbiased Evaluation

# Nested CV: inner loop tunes hyperparams, outer loop evaluates generalisation
# This avoids the optimistic bias of tuning and evaluating on the same data
set.seed(42)
outer_cv <- vfold_cv(train_baked, v = 5, strata = readmitted)
param_grid_small <- expand_grid(
  trees = c(100, 200), tree_depth = c(4, 6),
  learn_rate = c(0.05, 0.10), sample_size = 0.8
)

nested_auc <- map_dbl(seq_along(outer_cv$splits), function(fold) {
  sp <- outer_cv$splits[[fold]]
  d_in  <- analysis(sp)
  d_out <- assessment(sp)
  inner <- vfold_cv(d_in, v = 3, strata = readmitted)
  gs_inner <- tune_grid(
    xgb_wf, resamples = inner, grid = param_grid_small,
    metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
    control = control_grid(verbose = FALSE)
  )
  best <- select_best(gs_inner, metric = "roc_auc")
  fit  <- finalize_workflow(xgb_wf, best) %>% fit(d_in)
  p    <- predict(fit, new_data = d_out, type = "prob")$.pred_1
  auc_out <- auc_prob(as.integer(as.character(d_out$readmitted)), p)
  cat(sprintf("  Outer fold %d: best_params=%s | AUC=%.4f\n",
              fold, paste(names(best), best, sep = "=", collapse = ", "), auc_out))
  auc_out
})

4. Learning Curves

best_params <- select_best(gs, metric = "roc_auc")
best_wf <- finalize_workflow(xgb_wf, best_params)

train_fracs <- seq(0.10, 1.0, length.out = 10)
lc <- map_dfr(train_fracs, function(frac) {
  set.seed(42)
  n_use <- max(50, floor(frac * nrow(train_baked)))
  folds_lc <- vfold_cv(train_baked, v = 3, strata = readmitted)
  scores <- map(folds_lc$splits, function(sp) {
    tr <- analysis(sp)
    te <- assessment(sp)
    tr <- tr[sample.int(nrow(tr), min(n_use, nrow(tr))), ]
    fit <- best_wf %>% fit(tr)
    p_tr <- predict(fit, new_data = tr, type = "prob")$.pred_1
    p_te <- predict(fit, new_data = te, type = "prob")$.pred_1
    tibble(
      train = auc_prob(as.integer(as.character(tr$readmitted)), p_tr),
      val   = auc_prob(as.integer(as.character(te$readmitted)), p_te)
    )
  }) %>% bind_rows()
  tibble(
    n = n_use,
    train_mean = mean(scores$train), train_sd = sd(scores$train),
    val_mean   = mean(scores$val),   val_sd   = sd(scores$val)
  )
})

wbc  <- round(clip(rgamma(N, shape = 4 + 3 * immunocomp, scale = 2), 0.5, 40), 1)
lactate <- round(clip(rgamma(N, shape = 1.5 + 2 * immunocomp, scale = 0.8), 0.5, 15), 2)
creatinine <- round(clip(rgamma(N, shape = 1.6 + 0.8 * hf + 0.5 * ckd, scale = 0.6), 0.4, 12), 2)
n_comorb <- diabetes + hf + copd + ckd

# ── OUTCOME 1: Sepsis (high-recall binary) ────────────────────────────────────
sepsis_logit <- (-4.0 + 0.8 * immunocomp + 0.5 * as.integer(temp > 38.5) +
                   0.4 * as.integer(hr > 100) + 0.6 * as.integer(lactate > 2.0) +
                   0.5 * as.integer(wbc > 12) + 0.3 * as.integer(sbp < 90) +
                   0.3 * as.integer(resp > 22) + rnorm(N, 0, 0.3))
sepsis <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(sepsis_logit))

# ── OUTCOME 2: ICU LOS (regression) ──────────────────────────────────────────
icu_los <- round(clip(2.0 + 1.5 * sepsis + 1.2 * hf + 0.8 * ckd + 0.5 * copd +
                        0.04 * (age - 58) + 0.8 * as.integer(lactate > 2) +
                        0.5 * as.integer(sbp < 90) + rgamma(N, shape = 1.5, scale = 1.2),
                      1, 30), 1)

# ── OUTCOME 3: 30-day readmission (calibrated probability) ───────────────────
logit_re <- (-3.2 + 0.6 * hf + 0.5 * diabetes + 0.5 * ckd + 0.3 * copd +
               0.02 * (age - 58) / 15 + 0.3 * as.integer(icu_los > 7) +
               0.5 * hf * diabetes + rnorm(N, 0, 0.25))
readmitted <- rbinom(N, 1, sig(logit_re))

df <- tibble(
  age, sex, diabetes, hf, copd, ckd, immunocomp, n_comorb,
  temp, hr, sbp, resp, wbc, lactate, creatinine,
  sepsis, icu_los, readmitted
)
cat(sprintf("Dataset: %d x %d\n", nrow(df), ncol(df)))

Sepsis rate    : 4.9%

Mean ICU LOS   : 4.7 days (SD=1.8)

cat(sprintf("Readmission rate: %.1f%%\n", mean(readmitted) * 100))

Readmission rate: 8.0%

title: Three Clinical Prediction Models
text:
2. Model 1 — Sepsis Early Warning (High-Recall Classifier)
What does this section do?
This section introduces and explains the first example clinical prediction model: an early warning system for hospital sepsis built to prioritize high sensitivity. The goal is to develop a binary classifier that reliably identifies (predicts) patients who are developing or at risk for sepsis—an acute and potentially fatal medical condition.
Key points explained: - Why high recall?
In clinical workflows, missing a true case of sepsis (false negative) can have severe consequences for the patient. Thus, the model is tuned to maximize recall (sensitivity), meaning it will catch as many cases as possible, even if that produces more false positives (unnecessary alerts). - Features used:
The prediction is based on a combination of demographics, comorbidities, and real-time vital signs (like temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, labs). - Model and technical steps:
The workflow includes data preprocessing, imputation for missing values, normalization, and uses XGBoost for classification. The model’s decision threshold is specifically chosen to achieve at least 90% sensitivity on the validation data, ensuring most sepsis cases trigger an alert. - Metrics:
The explanation covers how AUC (a broad discrimination measure), average precision (helpful in imbalanced settings), and clinical-threshold sensitivity/specificity/PPV are reported. Special attention is given to the practical meaning of sensitivity (recall) for real-world deployment. - Clinical relevance:
The section underscores why such an approach—accepting more false alarms to reduce missed cases—is appropriate in high-stakes settings like sepsis detection. It helps learners appreciate the tradeoffs in applying ML to critical care, preparing them to set model thresholds according to actual clinical priorities and not just statistical optimization.
In summary, this model exemplifies how to align a machine learning classifier to critical clinical goals—here, minimizing missed sepsis by maximizing recall, and understanding the tradeoffs involved.

VITALS <- c("temp", "hr", "sbp", "resp", "wbc", "lactate", "creatinine", "age")
COMORB <- c("diabetes", "hf", "copd", "ckd", "immunocomp", "n_comorb")
SEPSIS_FEATURES <- c(VITALS, COMORB)

set.seed(42)
df_s <- df %>%
  select(all_of(c(SEPSIS_FEATURES, "sepsis"))) %>%
  mutate(sepsis = factor(sepsis, levels = c(0, 1)))
sp_s <- initial_split(df_s, prop = 0.80, strata = sepsis)
Xs_tr <- training(sp_s); Xs_te <- testing(sp_s)
ys_tr <- as.integer(as.character(Xs_tr$sepsis))
ys_te <- as.integer(as.character(Xs_te$sepsis))

rec_s <- recipe(sepsis ~ ., data = Xs_tr) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
pre_s <- prep(rec_s, training = Xs_tr)
Xstr <- as.matrix(bake(pre_s, new_data = Xs_tr) %>% select(-sepsis))
Xste <- as.matrix(bake(pre_s, new_data = Xs_te) %>% select(-sepsis))

# Use high recall objective: scale_pos_weight prioritises catching sepsis cases
gb_sepsis <- xgboost(
  data = Xstr, label = factor(ys_tr, levels = c(0, 1)), nrounds = 200, max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
  subsample = 0.8, objective = "binary:logistic", verbose = 0
)

# Choose high-sensitivity threshold (clinical: missing sepsis is costly)
roc_s <- pROC::roc(ys_te, prob_sepsis, quiet = TRUE)
tpr <- roc_s$sensitivities
fpr <- 1 - roc_s$specificities
thrs <- roc_s$thresholds
thrs[is.infinite(thrs)] <- ifelse(thrs[is.infinite(thrs)] > 0, 1, 0)
sens_target <- 0.90   # want to catch 90% of sepsis cases
idx90 <- which(tpr >= sens_target)
thr_highsens <- if (length(idx90)) thrs[idx90[1]] else 0.5
y_pred_s <- as.integer(prob_sepsis >= thr_highsens)
tp <- sum(y_pred_s == 1 & ys_te == 1); fp <- sum(y_pred_s == 1 & ys_te == 0)
tn <- sum(y_pred_s == 0 & ys_te == 0); fn <- sum(y_pred_s == 0 & ys_te == 1)

3. Model 2 — ICU Length-of-Stay Forecasting (Regression)
This section focuses on building a model to predict the length of stay (LOS) for patients in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), a numerical outcome best approached as a regression problem. Unlike classification (e.g., sepsis detection), here we estimate a continuous value—how many days a patient is likely to remain in the ICU—using clinical features such as vital signs, comorbidities, and indicators like sepsis.
We train an XGBoost regression model using these features, evaluate its performance with standard regression metrics (MAE, RMSE, R²), and examine the predictions and their errors. Additionally, we estimate approximate prediction intervals to understand the uncertainty of the model’s forecasts.

LOS_FEATURES <- c(VITALS, COMORB, "sepsis")
set.seed(42)
df_l <- df %>% select(all_of(c(LOS_FEATURES, "icu_los")))

  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

Xltr <- as.matrix(bake(pre_l, new_data = Xl_tr) %>% select(-icu_los))
Xlte <- as.matrix(bake(pre_l, new_data = Xl_te) %>% select(-icu_los))

gbr <- xgboost(
  data = Xltr, label = yl_tr, nrounds = 200, max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
  subsample = 0.8, objective = "reg:squarederror", verbose = 0
)

text:
4. Model 3 — 30-Day Readmission Risk Score (Calibrated)
This section introduces the third clinical prediction model: a 30-day readmission risk score built to provide a calibrated probability estimate for each patient. Unlike the previous models which focused on early warning or forecasting, this model estimates the probability of readmission within 30 days based on clinical features such as demographics, comorbidities, and hospital course (e.g., sepsis, ICU length of stay).
We train an XGBoost classifier with a binary logistic objective, evaluate its performance using AUC (area under the ROC curve) and Brier score (which measures calibration), and perform risk stratification into four tiers based on the predicted probability. Additionally, we apply Platt scaling to calibrate the raw model probabilities, improving their clinical interpretability and reliability.

RE_FEATURES <- c(VITALS, COMORB, "icu_los")
set.seed(42)
df_r <- df %>%
  select(all_of(c(RE_FEATURES, "readmitted"))) %>%
  mutate(readmitted = factor(readmitted, levels = c(0, 1)))
sp_r <- initial_split(df_r, prop = 0.80, strata = readmitted)
Xr_tr_all <- training(sp_r); Xr_te <- testing(sp_r)
sp_cal <- initial_split(Xr_tr_all, prop = 0.80, strata = readmitted)
Xr_tr2 <- training(sp_cal); Xr_cal <- testing(sp_cal)
yr_tr2 <- as.integer(as.character(Xr_tr2$readmitted))
yr_cal  <- as.integer(as.character(Xr_cal$readmitted))
yr_te   <- as.integer(as.character(Xr_te$readmitted))

rec_r <- recipe(readmitted ~ ., data = Xr_tr2) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
pre_r <- prep(rec_r, training = Xr_tr2)
Xrtr  <- as.matrix(bake(pre_r, new_data = Xr_tr2) %>% select(-readmitted))
Xrcal <- as.matrix(bake(pre_r, new_data = Xr_cal) %>% select(-readmitted))
Xrte  <- as.matrix(bake(pre_r, new_data = Xr_te)  %>% select(-readmitted))

gb_re <- xgboost(
  data = Xrtr, label = factor(yr_tr2, levels = c(0, 1)), nrounds = 200, max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
  subsample = 0.8, objective = "binary:logistic", verbose = 0
)

title: Three Clinical Prediction Models
text:
5. Three-Model Deployment Summary
This section summarizes the three clinical prediction models built in previous sections: sepsis early warning, ICU length-of-stay forecasting, and 30-day readmission risk scoring. It provides a comprehensive overview of how these models were developed, evaluated, and deployed in a real-world clinical setting.
Key points explained: - Model 1: Sepsis Early Warning
This model is designed to alert healthcare professionals when a patient is at high risk of developing sepsis, a severe and potentially life-threatening condition. It uses a high-sensitivity threshold to minimize missed cases, even at the cost of increased false alarms. - Model 2: ICU Length-of-Stay Forecasting
This model estimates how many days a patient is likely to remain in the ICU, useful for bed management and resource allocation. It provides a continuous prediction rather than a binary alert. - Model 3: 30-Day Readmission Risk Score
This model estimates the probability of readmission within 30 days, helping identify patients who may benefit from early intervention programs. It uses Platt scaling to improve calibration and risk stratification.
Deployment checklist:
The section includes a checklist of key considerations for deploying these models in a clinical setting, including threshold selection, model calibration, and risk stratification guidelines.

pr_s <- yardstick::pr_curve(
  tibble(truth = factor(ys_te, levels = c(0, 1)), .pred = prob_sepsis),
  truth, .pred, event_level = "second"

  geom_path(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(ys_te), colour = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.90, colour = col_green, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Recall", y = "Precision",
       title = sprintf("Model 1: Sepsis\n(Precision-Recall, AP=%.3f)", ap_s))

los_bins <- cut(yl_te, c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30), labels = c("1-3d", "4-7d", "8-14d", ">14d"))
mae_by_bin <- tibble(bin = los_bins, actual = yl_te, pred = pred_los) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  summarise(mae = mean(abs(actual - pred)), .groups = "drop")
p2 <- ggplot(mae_by_bin, aes(bin, mae, fill = bin)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1fd", mae)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_green, col_gold, col_red)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "MAE (days)",
       title = sprintf("Model 2: ICU LOS\nMAE by LOS stratum (overall=%.2fd)", mae))

  tibble(y = y, p = p) %>%
    mutate(bin = ntile(p, n_bins)) %>%

}
cal <- bind_rows(

       title = "Model 3: Readmission\nCalibration (before/after Platt)") +

6. Knowledge Check

After Platt recalibration the readmission model Brier score improves. Explain what recalibration does.

Combine all three models into a patient risk dashboard: for each patient, output sepsis alert, expected LOS, and readmission probability tier.


# Exercise 5 — patient dashboard
patient_risk_dashboard <- function(patient_row) {
  # Return sepsis alert, expected LOS, readmission tier for one patient.
  Xs <- as.matrix(bake(pre_s, new_data = as_tibble(patient_row[SEPSIS_FEATURES])) %>%
                    select(-any_of("sepsis")))
  Xl <- as.matrix(bake(pre_l, new_data = as_tibble(patient_row[LOS_FEATURES])) %>%
                    select(-any_of("icu_los")))
  Xr <- as.matrix(bake(pre_r, new_data = as_tibble(patient_row[RE_FEATURES])) %>%
                    select(-any_of("readmitted")))
  p_sepsis <- predict(gb_sepsis, Xs)
  p_los    <- predict(gbr, Xl)
  p_re_raw <- predict(gb_re, Xr)
  p_re_cal <- as.numeric(predict(platt, newdata = tibble(p = p_re_raw), type = "response"))
  tier <- dplyr::case_when(
    p_re_cal < 0.10 ~ "Low",
    p_re_cal < 0.20 ~ "Moderate",
    p_re_cal < 0.35 ~ "High",
    TRUE ~ "Very high"
  )
  list(sepsis_alert = p_sepsis >= thr_highsens, sepsis_prob = round(p_sepsis, 3),
       expected_los = round(p_los, 1), readmit_prob = round(p_re_cal, 3),
       readmit_tier = tier)

text:
3. Clinical Abbreviation Expansion

clinical_abbrevs <- c(
  DM2  = "type 2 diabetes mellitus",
  HTN  = "hypertension",
  CKD  = "chronic kidney disease",
  HF   = "heart failure",
  CAD  = "coronary artery disease",
  COPD = "chronic obstructive pulmonary disease",
  PE   = "pulmonary embolism",
  SOB  = "shortness of breath",
  CP   = "chest pain",
  LE   = "lower extremity",
  `c/o` = "complaining of",
  `h/o` = "history of",
  PMH  = "past medical history",
  `s/p` = "status post",
  Pt   = "patient",
  pt   = "patient",
  HR   = "heart rate",
  BP   = "blood pressure",
  RR   = "respiratory rate",
  SpO2 = "oxygen saturation",
  EF   = "ejection fraction",
  BNP  = "brain natriuretic peptide",
  A1c  = "hemoglobin A1c",
  PO   = "by mouth",
  IV   = "intravenous",
  BID  = "twice daily",
  QD   = "once daily",
  QAM  = "every morning",
  q4h  = "every 4 hours",
  q8h  = "every 8 hours",
  EKG  = "electrocardiogram",
  CXR  = "chest X-ray",
  ABG  = "arterial blood gas",
  ECHO = "echocardiogram",
  NTG  = "nitroglycerin",
  ASA  = "aspirin",
  Cr   = "creatinine",
  BUN  = "blood urea nitrogen",
  NC   = "nasal cannula"
)

expand_abbreviations <- function(text, abbrev_dict = clinical_abbrevs) {
  # Longest abbreviations first so "DM2" is not split by "DM"
  ord <- order(nchar(names(abbrev_dict)), decreasing = TRUE)
  for (i in ord) {
    abbrev <- names(abbrev_dict)[i]
    expansion <- unname(abbrev_dict[i])
    pattern <- paste0("\\b", stringr::str_replace_all(abbrev, "([\\W])", "\\\\\\1"), "\\b")
    text <- stringr::str_replace_all(text, stringr::regex(pattern), expansion)
  }
  text
}

6. Vital Signs & Lab Value Extraction

vital_patterns <- c(
  temperature    = "T\\s*(?:emp)?\\s*:?\\s*(\\d{2,3}\\.?\\d?)\\s*[CF]?",
  heart_rate     = "HR\\s*:?\\s*(\\d{2,3})\\s*(?:bpm)?",
  blood_pressure = "BP\\s*:?\\s*(\\d{2,3})\\s*/\\s*(\\d{2,3})",
  resp_rate      = "RR\\s*:?\\s*(\\d{1,2})",
  spo2           = "SpO2\\s*:?\\s*(\\d{2,3})\\s*%"
)
lab_patterns <- c(
  sodium        = "Na\\s*(\\d{3})",
  potassium     = "K\\s*(\\d\\.\\d)",
  creatinine    = "Cr\\s*(\\d\\.\\d)",
  bnp           = "BNP\\s*(\\d{2,5})",
  troponin_i    = "Troponin\\s*I\\s*:?\\s*(\\d+\\.\\d+)",
  ejection_frac = "EF\\s*(\\d{2})\\s*%"
)

extract_vitals_labs <- function(text) {
  results <- list()
  all_pats <- c(vital_patterns, lab_patterns)
  for (name in names(all_pats)) {
    m <- stringr::str_match(text, stringr::regex(all_pats[[name]], ignore_case = TRUE))
    if (!is.na(m[1, 1])) {
      if (name == "blood_pressure") {
        results$systolic  <- as.numeric(m[1, 2])
        results$diastolic <- as.numeric(m[1, 3])
      } else {
        val <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(m[1, 2]))
        results[[name]] <- if (!is.na(val)) val else m[1, 2]
      }
    }
  }
  results
}

8. Full Preprocessing Pipeline

preprocess_clinical_note <- function(text, note_id = "") {
  result <- list(note_id = note_id, original_length = nchar(text))
  result$phi_detected  <- detect_phi(text)
  clean <- deidentify(text)
  result$expanded_text <- expand_abbreviations(clean)
  result$sections      <- extract_sections(text)
  result$vitals_labs   <- extract_vitals_labs(text)
  lines <- stringr::str_split(result$expanded_text, "\n")[[1]]
  sentences <- lines[nchar(stringr::str_squish(lines)) > 0]
  sentences <- sentences[purrr::map_int(stringr::str_split(sentences, "\\s+"), length) > 5]
  result$sentences      <- sentences
  result$sentence_count <- length(sentences)
  result
}

text:
9. Medication Extraction Exercise

med_pattern <- paste0(
  "(\\d+\\.\\s+)?([A-Z][a-zA-Z]+(?:\\s+[a-zA-Z]+)?)",
  "\\s+(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?\\s*(?:mg|mcg|g|mL|units?))",
  "(?:\\s+((?:PO|IV|SQ|IM)\\s+(?:BID|QD|TID|QAM|q\\d+h)))?"
)

extract_medications <- function(text) {
  m <- stringr::str_match_all(text, stringr::regex(med_pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))[[1]]
  if (nrow(m) == 0) {
    return(tibble::tibble(drug = character(), dose = character(), route_freq = character()))
  }
  tibble::tibble(
    drug       = stringr::str_squish(m[, 3]),
    dose       = stringr::str_squish(m[, 4]),
    route_freq = stringr::str_squish(ifelse(is.na(m[, 5]), "", m[, 5]))
  )
}

purrr::pwalk(df_notes, function(note_id, text, ...) {
  meds <- extract_medications(text)
  if (nrow(meds) > 0) {
    cat(sprintf("%s:\n", note_id))
    purrr::pwalk(meds, function(drug, dose, route_freq) {
      cat(sprintf("  %-20s %-12s %s\n", drug, dose, route_freq))
    })
  }
})

augment <- function(text, noise = 0.15) {
  words <- strsplit(text, "\\s+")[[1]]
  extra <- c("assessment", "plan", "patient", "stable", "monitor", "admitted")
  result <- character()
  for (w in words) {
    result <- c(result, w)
    if (runif(1) < noise) result <- c(result, sample(extra, 1))
  }
  paste(result, collapse = " ")
}

    pred <- predict(tmod, newdata = dte)
    proba <- as.numeric(predict(tmod, newdata = dte, type = "probability")[, "1"])
    list(name = name, proba = proba, pred = as.integer(as.character(pred)))
  } else {
    fit <- glmnet::glmnet(xtr, yr_tr, family = family, alpha = alpha,
                          lambda = 0.01, maxit = 2000)
    proba <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newx = xte, type = "response"))
    pred  <- as.integer(proba >= 0.5)
    list(name = name, proba = proba, pred = pred)
  }
}

3. Sentence Embeddings
Working analogue of sentence-transformers: TF-IDF document-feature matrix + truncated SVD (LSA) yields dense 64-d embeddings. Same downstream tasks as BERT sentence embeddings (cosine similarity, PCA, zero-shot).

embed_texts <- function(texts, n_comp = 64, train_dfm = NULL, svd_fit = NULL) {
  texts <- as.character(texts)
  names(texts) <- paste0("doc", seq_along(texts))
  toks <- quanteda::tokens(texts, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
    quanteda::tokens_tolower() |>
    quanteda::tokens_ngrams(n = 1:2)
  d <- quanteda::dfm(toks)
  if (is.null(train_dfm)) {
    d <- quanteda::dfm_tfidf(d)
    n_comp <- min(n_comp, nfeat(d) - 1, ndoc(d) - 1)
    mat <- as.matrix(d)
    svd_fit <- svd(mat, nu = n_comp, nv = n_comp)
    embeddings <- svd_fit$u %*% diag(svd_fit$d[seq_len(n_comp)])
    list(embeddings = embeddings, dfm = d, svd = svd_fit)
  } else {
    d <- quanteda::dfm_match(d, features = quanteda::featnames(train_dfm))
    d <- quanteda::dfm_tfidf(d)
    mat <- as.matrix(d)
    n_comp <- ncol(svd_fit$v)
    embeddings <- mat %*% svd_fit$v[, seq_len(n_comp), drop = FALSE]
    list(embeddings = embeddings, dfm = d, svd = svd_fit)
  }
}

# Cosine similarity matrix
cosine_matrix <- function(X) {
  nrms <- sqrt(rowSums(X^2))
  nrms[nrms == 0] <- 1
  Xn <- X / nrms
  tcrossprod(Xn)
}

text:
3. LSA-Based Summarisation

lsa_summarise <- function(text, n_sents = 5, n_comp = 4) {
  sents <- split_sentences(text)
  if (length(sents) <= n_sents) return(sents)
  d <- sentence_tfidf(sents)
  X <- as.matrix(d)
  n_comp <- min(n_comp, nrow(X) - 1, ncol(X) - 1)
  if (n_comp < 1) return(sents[seq_len(n_sents)])
  svd_fit <- svd(X, nu = n_comp, nv = n_comp)
  X_r <- svd_fit$u %*% diag(svd_fit$d[seq_len(n_comp)], n_comp, n_comp)
  scs <- sqrt(rowSums(X_r^2))
  top_idx <- sort(order(scs, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sents)])
  sents[top_idx]
}

lsa_sents <- lsa_summarise(discharge_summary, n_sents = 5)

title: Summarisation & Zero-Shot NLP
text:
4. Section-Aware Summarisation

section_weights <- c(
  "DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES"   = 3.0,
  "DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS" = 2.5,
  "HOSPITAL COURSE"       = 2.0,
  "FOLLOW-UP"             = 1.5,
  "LABS"                  = 1.0,
  "ADMITTING DIAGNOSIS"   = 1.0,
  "DISCHARGE CONDITION"   = 1.5
)

get_section <- function(pos, text) {
  best <- "GENERAL"
  best_pos <- -1
  for (header in names(section_weights)) {
    hp <- regexpr(header, toupper(text), fixed = TRUE)[1]
    if (hp != -1 && hp < pos && hp > best_pos) {
      best <- header
      best_pos <- hp
    }
  }
  best
}

section_aware_summarise <- function(text, n_sents = 6) {
  sents <- split_sentences(text)
  if (length(sents) <= n_sents) {
    return(list(sents = sents, secs = rep("GENERAL", length(sents))))
  }
  d <- sentence_tfidf(sents)
  ts <- as.numeric(rowSums(as.matrix(d)))
  weighted <- numeric(length(sents))
  secs <- character(length(sents))
  for (i in seq_along(sents)) {
    pos <- regexpr(sents[i], text, fixed = TRUE)[1]
    if (pos == -1) pos <- 1
    sec <- get_section(pos, text)
    w <- if (sec %in% names(section_weights)) section_weights[[sec]] else 0.5
    weighted[i] <- ts[i] * w
    secs[i] <- sec
  }
  top_idx <- sort(order(weighted, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sents)])
  list(sents = sents[top_idx], secs = secs[top_idx])
}

sa <- section_aware_summarise(discharge_summary, n_sents = 6)
cat("Section-Aware Summary (6 sentences):\n\n")

  cat(sprintf("  [%-22s] %s\n",

title: Summarisation & Zero-Shot NLP
text:
7. Zero-Shot TF-IDF Triage Classifier
Keyword / label similarity analogue of zero-shot NLI: cosine similarity between the note and triage-class descriptions.

triage_descs <- c(
  IMMEDIATE   = paste("cardiac arrest respiratory failure unresponsive SpO2 below 85 BP below 70",
                      "active hemorrhage STEMI severe respiratory distress cyanosis anaphylaxis"),
  URGENT      = paste("chest pain active angina dyspnea rest SpO2 92 altered mental status",
                      "new neurological deficit uncontrolled pain severe hypertension fever sepsis"),
  SEMI_URGENT = paste("moderate pain stable vital signs mild dyspnea worsening chronic condition",
                      "urinary symptoms mild infection stable arrhythmia elevated glucose"),
  ROUTINE     = paste("prescription refill follow-up chronic stable lab results review",
                      "medication adjustment preventive care no acute distress")
)

zero_shot_triage <- function(text) {
  all_texts <- c(unname(triage_descs), text)
  toks <- quanteda::tokens(all_texts, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
    quanteda::tokens_tolower() |>
    quanteda::tokens_ngrams(n = 1:2)
  d <- quanteda::dfm_tfidf(quanteda::dfm(toks))
  mat <- as.matrix(d)
  nrms <- sqrt(rowSums(mat^2)); nrms[nrms == 0] <- 1
  Xn <- mat / nrms
  scores <- as.numeric(Xn[nrow(Xn), ] %*% t(Xn[-nrow(Xn), , drop = FALSE]))
  names(scores) <- names(triage_descs)
  sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
}

  "Patient found unresponsive, no pulse, CPR initiated.",
  "67yo chest pain 7/10 radiating to left arm, diaphoretic, EKG ST elevation.",
  "45yo BP 190/110, severe headache, visual changes, no focal neuro deficit.",
  "72yo increasing shortness of breath x3 days, orthopnea, bilateral leg swelling.",

title: Summarisation & Zero-Shot NLP
text:
8. Knowledge Check

TextRank ROUGE-1 F1=0.42. What baseline would you compare against (e.g. lead-1)?
The section-aware method weighted DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES at 3.0. What justifies this?
Zero-shot triage classified chest pain as SEMI-URGENT. What safety implications?
Abstractive LLM summarisation can hallucinate clinical facts. Describe two validation strategies.
Implement a lead-1 baseline: use the first sentence of each major section.


lead_baseline <- function(text) {
  headers <- c("ADMITTING DIAGNOSIS", "HOSPITAL COURSE", "DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES",
               "DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS", "FOLLOW-UP", "DISCHARGE CONDITION")
  sents <- character()
  for (h in headers) {
    pos <- regexpr(h, toupper(text), fixed = TRUE)[1]
    if (pos == -1) next
    rest <- substr(text, pos, min(nchar(text), pos + 299))
    for (line in strsplit(rest, "\\.")[[1]]) {
      line <- stringr::str_squish(line)
      if (length(strsplit(line, "\\s+")[[1]]) > 5) {
        sents <- c(sents, paste0(line, "."))
        break
      }
    }
  }
  sents
}

lead_sents <- lead_baseline(discharge_summary)
hyp_lead <- paste(lead_sents, collapse = " ")
rl <- rouge_l(hyp_lead, reference)

cat(sprintf("Lead-section baseline: ROUGE-1 F1=%.4f | ROUGE-L F1=%.4f\n\n", r1$f1, rl$f1))

title: DAGs, Confounding & Identification
text:
1. Setup & Shared Dataset

library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
)

mod06_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mod06")
dir.create(mod06_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

col_blue  <- "#2563EB"
col_red   <- "#DC2626"
col_green <- "#16A34A"

logistic <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

set.seed(42)
N <- 5000

# Confounders
age          <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 60, 12), 30), 90)
smoking      <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(-1 + 0.02 * (age - 60)))
chd_history  <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(-2 + 0.03 * (age - 60)))
ldl_baseline <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 140 + 20 * smoking, 30), 60), 280)
ses_score    <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # socioeconomic (higher=better)

# Treatment: statin use (confounded by LDL, CHD, age, SES)
statin_logit <- (-2.0 + 0.025 * (ldl_baseline - 140) + 1.0 * chd_history
                 + 0.02 * (age - 60) - 0.3 * ses_score)
statin <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(statin_logit))

# True causal effect: statin reduces MI risk (log-odds = -0.8)
TRUE_EFFECT <- -0.8
mi_logit <- (-3.0 + TRUE_EFFECT * statin + 0.03 * (age - 60)
             + 0.5 * smoking + 0.8 * chd_history + 0.005 * (ldl_baseline - 140))
mi <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(mi_logit))

df <- tibble(
  age          = age,
  smoking      = smoking,
  chd_history  = chd_history,
  ldl_baseline = ldl_baseline,
  ses_score    = ses_score,
  statin       = statin,
  mi           = mi
)
COVARIATES <- c("age", "smoking", "chd_history", "ldl_baseline", "ses_score")
TREATMENT  <- "statin"
OUTCOME    <- "mi"

cat(sprintf("N=%d | Statin=%.1f%% | MI rate=%.1f%%\n",
            N, mean(statin) * 100, mean(mi) * 100))

N=5000 | Statin=18.7% | MI rate=7.1%

cat(sprintf("True log-odds effect: %s | True OR: %.3f\n",
            TRUE_EFFECT, exp(TRUE_EFFECT)))

True log-odds effect: -0.8 | True OR: 0.449

title: DAGs, Confounding & Identification
text:
2. Association vs Causation
Potential Outcomes Framework (Rubin, 1974): - Y(1) = outcome if treated | Y(0) = outcome if untreated - Individual causal effect = Y(1) - Y(0) — never directly observed (fundamental problem) - ATE = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]
Key structural variable types:



Type
DAG pattern
Action




Confounder
C → T and C → Y
Must adjust


Mediator
T → M → Y
Do NOT adjust (blocks causal path)


Collider
T → C ← Y
Do NOT adjust (opens spurious path)


Instrument
Z → T, Z ⊥ Y given T
Use for IV estimation

  SES [pos="0,-1"]

  SES -> Statin

}
')

3. Naive vs Adjusted Effect Estimation

# Naive (ignores confounding)
fit_naive <- glm(mi ~ statin, data = df, family = binomial())
naive_coef <- coef(fit_naive)[["statin"]]

# Adjusted (backdoor adjustment)
fit_adj <- glm(
  mi ~ statin + age + smoking + chd_history + ldl_baseline + ses_score,
  data = df, family = binomial()
)
adj_coef <- coef(fit_adj)[["statin"]]

cat(sprintf("True effect         : %.3f  (OR = %.3f)\n",
            TRUE_EFFECT, exp(TRUE_EFFECT)))

            naive_coef, exp(naive_coef)))

title: DAGs, Confounding & Identification
text:
4. Collider Bias Demonstration

# Among hospitalised patients: smoking & alcohol appear correlated
# In truth they are independent — conditioning on hospitalisation (collider) opens bias
set.seed(7)
N_col <- 3000
smoking_c  <- rnorm(N_col)
alcohol_c  <- rnorm(N_col)   # truly independent of smoking
hosp_score <- 0.6 * smoking_c + 0.6 * alcohol_c + rnorm(N_col, 0, 0.5)
hospitalised <- as.integer(hosp_score > quantile(hosp_score, 0.75))

title: Difference-in-Differences & Event Studies
text:
2. Classic 2×2 DiD — Medicaid Expansion Example
Scenario: State Medicaid expansion under ACA (2014). Some states expanded (treated), others did not (control). Outcome: uninsured rate per county.
DiD Estimator:
DiD = (Y_treat_post - Y_treat_pre) - (Y_ctrl_post - Y_ctrl_pre)
Assumption: Parallel trends — absent the policy, treated and control states would have followed the same trend in the outcome.

# Simulate Medicaid expansion data (state-level panel, 2012-2017)
set.seed(42)
N_states    <- 50
T_periods   <- 6      # 2012-2017
POLICY_YEAR <- 2014   # ACA Medicaid expansion
years       <- 2012:2017

# 25 states expand, 25 don't
expanded <- c(rep(1, 25), rep(0, 25))
state_fe <- rnorm(N_states, 0, 2)  # state fixed effects
# True ATT: expansion reduces uninsured rate by 4 percentage points
TRUE_ATT <- -4.0

records <- vector("list", N_states * length(years))
idx <- 1
for (s in seq_len(N_states)) {
  for (yr in years) {
    post  <- as.integer(yr >= POLICY_YEAR)
    treat <- expanded[s]
    # Pre-trend (same slope for both)
    trend <- -0.8 * (yr - 2012)  # national trend: uninsured falling
    # Treatment effect only for treated states after policy
    effect <- TRUE_ATT * treat * post
    # Base uninsured rate + state FE + trend + effect + noise
    uninsured <- (18 + state_fe[s] + trend + effect + 3 * treat
                  + rnorm(1, 0, 1.5))
    records[[idx]] <- tibble(
      state = s, year = yr, expanded = treat,
      post = post, uninsured_pct = uninsured
    )
    idx <- idx + 1
  }
}
df_did <- bind_rows(records)

cat(sprintf("DiD panel: %d state-years | %d states | %d years\n",
            nrow(df_did), N_states, T_periods))

DiD panel: 300 state-years | 50 states | 6 years

cat(sprintf("Expansion states: %d | Non-expansion: %d\n",
            sum(expanded), sum(1 - expanded)))

Expansion states: 25 | Non-expansion: 25

# 2x2 DiD table
dd_table <- df_did |>
  group_by(expanded, post) |>
  summarise(mean_unins = mean(uninsured_pct), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    group = if_else(expanded == 1, "Expansion", "Non-expansion"),
    period = if_else(post == 1, "Post-policy (2014-17)", "Pre-policy (2012-13)")
  ) |>
  select(group, period, mean_unins) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = mean_unins)

cat("\n2x2 DiD Table:\n")


2x2 DiD Table:

print(dd_table |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))))

  <chr>                          <dbl>                   <dbl>
1 Non-expansion                   17.3                    14.5

y_t_pre  <- dd_table[["Pre-policy (2012-13)"]][dd_table$group == "Expansion"]

# Regression DiD: Y = alpha + beta1*Treat + beta2*Post + beta3*(Treat*Post) + FE + e

# Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) with fixest (clustered by state)
model_twfe <- feols(
  uninsured_pct ~ expanded:post | state + year,
  data = df_did,
  cluster = ~state
)

did_coef <- coef(model_twfe)[["expanded:post"]]
did_ci   <- confint(model_twfe)["expanded:post", ]
did_se   <- se(model_twfe)[["expanded:post"]]

cat("Two-Way Fixed Effects DiD (fixest):\n")

Two-Way Fixed Effects DiD (fixest):

  True ATT       : -4.0 pp

cat(sprintf("  Bias           : %+.3f pp\n", did_coef - TRUE_ATT))

)
ct_lm <- coeftest(model_lm, vcov. = vcovCL(model_lm, cluster = df_did$state))

  group_by(year, expanded) |>

  mutate(group = if_else(expanded == 1, "Expansion", "Non-expansion"))

  arrange(year)

    x = "Year", y = "Uninsured rate (%)", colour = NULL,

  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +

text:
5. Staggered Adoption — Callaway-Sant’Anna

# When treatment rolls out at different times, naive TWFE gives
# a weighted average that can be negative even when all cohort ATTs are positive
# Callaway-Sant'Anna (2021) estimates cohort-specific ATTs

set.seed(42)
N_states2 <- 60
cohorts <- c(2014, 2015, 2016, NA)  # NA = never-treated
cohort_assign <- rep(cohorts, each = 15)
TRUE_COHORT_ATT <- c(`2014` = -5.0, `2015` = -4.0, `2016` = -3.0)  # heterogeneous effects

state_fe2 <- rnorm(N_states2, 0, 2)
records2 <- vector("list", N_states2 * length(2012:2019))
idx <- 1
for (s in seq_len(N_states2)) {
  cohort <- cohort_assign[s]
  for (yr in 2012:2019) {
    post <- !is.na(cohort) && yr >= cohort
    effect <- if (post) unname(TRUE_COHORT_ATT[as.character(cohort)]) else 0
    unins <- (18 + state_fe2[s] - 0.8 * (yr - 2012) + effect
              + rnorm(1, 0, 1.5))
    records2[[idx]] <- tibble(
      state = s, year = yr,
      cohort = if (is.na(cohort)) "None" else as.character(cohort),
      treated = as.integer(!is.na(cohort)),
      post = as.integer(post),
      uninsured_pct = unins
    )
    idx <- idx + 1
  }
}
df_staggered <- bind_rows(records2)

# Simple cohort-specific DiD (Callaway-Sant'Anna principle)
# Compare each treated cohort to never-treated states in the relevant period
never_treated <- df_staggered |> filter(cohort == "None")
cs_results <- list()
ri <- 1
for (g in c("2014", "2015", "2016")) {
  g_int <- as.integer(g)
  cohort_data <- df_staggered |> filter(cohort == g)
  for (t in g_int:2019) {
    mu_g_t     <- mean(cohort_data$uninsured_pct[cohort_data$year == t])
    mu_g_base  <- mean(cohort_data$uninsured_pct[cohort_data$year == g_int - 1])
    mu_nt_t    <- mean(never_treated$uninsured_pct[never_treated$year == t])
    mu_nt_base <- mean(never_treated$uninsured_pct[never_treated$year == g_int - 1])
    att_gt <- (mu_g_t - mu_g_base) - (mu_nt_t - mu_nt_base)
    cs_results[[ri]] <- tibble(
      cohort = g, year = t, att = att_gt,
      true_att = unname(TRUE_COHORT_ATT[g])
    )
    ri <- ri + 1
  }
}
df_cs <- bind_rows(cs_results)

true_lines <- tibble(
  cohort = names(TRUE_COHORT_ATT),
  true_att = unname(TRUE_COHORT_ATT)
)

p_cs <- ggplot(df_cs, aes(x = year, y = att, colour = cohort)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(
    data = true_lines, aes(yintercept = true_att, colour = cohort),
    linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("2014" = col_red, "2015" = col_blue,
                                 "2016" = col_green)) +
  labs(
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "ATT(g,t) — pp reduction in uninsured rate",
    colour = "Cohort",
    title = "Callaway-Sant'Anna: Cohort-specific ATTs (dotted = true effect for each cohort)"
  )

print(p_cs)







ggsave(file.path(mod06_dir, "cs_did.png"), p_cs,
       width = 11, height = 5, dpi = 120)

# Aggregate ATT
agg_att <- df_cs |>
  group_by(cohort) |>
  summarise(att = mean(att), .groups = "drop")

cat("Callaway-Sant'Anna Aggregate ATTs:\n")

Callaway-Sant'Anna Aggregate ATTs:

for (g in c("2014", "2015", "2016")) {
  est <- agg_att$att[agg_att$cohort == g]
  cat(sprintf("  Cohort %s: Est=%.2f pp | True=%.1f pp\n",
              g, est, TRUE_COHORT_ATT[g]))
}

title: Instrumental Variables & RDD
text:
2. Instrumental Variables — Distance to Hospital
Scenario: Does receiving cardiac catheterisation cause lower mortality? - Problem: sicker patients are more likely to receive the procedure (confounding) - Instrument: Distance to nearest catheterisation-capable hospital - Relevance: Patients closer to cath-capable hospitals more likely to receive cath - Exclusion: Distance affects mortality ONLY through cath (not through other paths) - Independence: Distance is as-good-as-random (not correlated with patient severity)
2SLS Estimator: 1. First stage: Cath = alpha + gammaZ + Xdelta + v 2. Second stage: Mortality = beta0 + beta1Cath_hat + Xpi + e

# Simulate cardiac catheterisation data
set.seed(42)
N <- 3000

# Instrument: distance to nearest cath hospital (miles)
distance <- pmin(pmax(rexp(N, rate = 1 / 25), 1), 120)

# Unobserved severity (the confounder — related to treatment but not instrument)
severity <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)

# Treatment: cardiac catheterisation (influenced by both distance and severity)
cath_logit <- 1.5 - 0.03 * distance + 0.8 * severity + rnorm(N, 0, 0.5)
cath <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(cath_logit))

# Covariates
age <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(N, 65, 12), 30), 90)
ami <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.6)  # acute MI

# Outcome: 30-day mortality
TRUE_CATH_EFFECT <- -0.5  # log-odds cath reduces mortality
mortality_logit <- (-2.0 + TRUE_CATH_EFFECT * cath + 0.5 * severity
                    + 0.02 * (age - 65) + 0.4 * ami + rnorm(N, 0, 0.4))
mortality <- rbinom(N, 1, logistic(mortality_logit))

df_iv <- tibble(
  distance  = distance,
  severity  = severity,
  cath      = cath,
  age       = age,
  ami       = ami,
  mortality = mortality
)

cat(sprintf("N=%d | Cath rate=%.1f%% | Mortality=%.1f%%\n",
            N, mean(cath) * 100, mean(mortality) * 100))

N=3000 | Cath rate=65.1% | Mortality=13.8%

cat("Cath rate by distance quartile:\n")

Cath rate by distance quartile:

bounds <- list(c(0, 25), c(25, 40), c(40, 60), c(60, 130))
for (q in seq_along(bounds)) {
  lo <- bounds[[q]][1]; hi <- bounds[[q]][2]
  sub <- df_iv |> filter(distance >= lo, distance < hi)
  cat(sprintf("  Q%d (%d-%d miles): %.1f%% cath | %.1f%% mort\n",
              q, lo, hi, mean(sub$cath) * 100, mean(sub$mortality) * 100))
}

  Q1 (0-25 miles): 73.0% cath | 13.5% mort
  Q2 (25-40 miles): 61.9% cath | 14.2% mort
  Q3 (40-60 miles): 53.4% cath | 14.1% mort
  Q4 (60-130 miles): 30.6% cath | 14.9% mort



# OLS (NAIVE — biased due to severity confounding)
model_ols <- lm(mortality ~ cath + age + ami, data = df_iv)
ols_coef  <- unname(coef(model_ols)[["cath"]])

# First stage: Cath ~ Distance + Covariates  (manual 2SLS)
fs_model <- lm(cath ~ distance + age + ami, data = df_iv)
fs_sum   <- summary(fs_model)
f_stat   <- unname(fs_sum$fstatistic["value"])
cath_hat <- fitted(fs_model)
cat(sprintf("First stage F-statistic: %.1f  (%s instrument, threshold = 10)\n",
            f_stat, if (f_stat > 10) "Strong" else "Weak"))

First stage F-statistic: 90.7  (Strong instrument, threshold = 10)

cat(sprintf("First stage coefficient on distance: %.4f (should be negative)\n",
            coef(fs_model)[["distance"]]))

First stage coefficient on distance: -0.0057 (should be negative)

# Partial F on the excluded instrument (preferred strength diagnostic)
fs_reduced <- lm(cath ~ age + ami, data = df_iv)
partial_f  <- anova(fs_reduced, fs_model)$F[2]
cat(sprintf("Partial F (distance | covariates): %.1f\n", partial_f))

Partial F (distance | covariates): 272.1

# Second stage: Mortality ~ Cath_hat + Covariates (manual 2SLS)
df_iv$cath_hat <- cath_hat
model_2sls <- lm(mortality ~ cath_hat + age + ami, data = df_iv)
iv_coef    <- unname(coef(model_2sls)[["cath_hat"]])

# ivreg 2SLS (correct SEs; first-stage F via diagnostics)
iv_fit <- ivreg(mortality ~ cath + age + ami | distance + age + ami, data = df_iv)
iv_sum <- summary(iv_fit, diagnostics = TRUE)
ivreg_coef <- unname(coef(iv_fit)[["cath"]])
weak_f <- tryCatch(

title: Instrumental Variables & RDD
text:
3. Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
Scenario: Patients with LDL >= 190 mg/dL receive statin therapy per guidelines. Patients just below 190 do not.
The cutoff creates quasi-random assignment: patients just above and below 190 are similar on all characteristics, but differ in treatment probability.
Sharp RDD: Exact compliance at cutoff (everyone above gets treated)
Fuzzy RDD: Probability of treatment jumps at cutoff (imperfect compliance)

# Simulate LDL-based statin RDD
set.seed(42)
N_rdd  <- 2000
CUTOFF <- 190  # LDL mg/dL guideline threshold

ldl <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(N_rdd, 185, 20), 130), 250)
above_cutoff <- as.integer(ldl >= CUTOFF)
severity_rdd <- rnorm(N_rdd, 0, 1)

# SHARP RDD: treatment perfectly determined by cutoff
statin_sharp <- above_cutoff

# FUZZY RDD: probability jumps at cutoff but not perfectly
statin_prob  <- logistic(-2 + 5 * above_cutoff + 0.5 * rnorm(N_rdd, 0, 1))
statin_fuzzy <- rbinom(N_rdd, 1, statin_prob)

# Outcome: cardiovascular event (5 years)
TRUE_RDD_EFFECT <- -0.15  # risk difference
cv_prob <- 0.25 + TRUE_RDD_EFFECT * statin_sharp - 0.002 * (ldl - 190) + 0.05 * severity_rdd
cv_prob <- pmin(pmax(cv_prob, 0.01), 0.99)
cv_event <- rbinom(N_rdd, 1, cv_prob)

df_rdd <- tibble(
  ldl          = ldl,
  above        = above_cutoff,
  statin_sharp = statin_sharp,
  statin_fuzzy = statin_fuzzy,
  cv_event     = cv_event,
  severity     = severity_rdd
) |>
  mutate(running = ldl - CUTOFF)  # centered at cutoff

cat(sprintf("CV event rate: %.1f%%\n", mean(cv_event) * 100))

# Sharp RDD estimation with local linear regression
BANDWIDTH <- 15  # optimal bandwidth (in practice: use data-driven methods)

rdd_estimate <- function(df, running_col, outcome_col, bw) {
  in_bw <- df[abs(df[[running_col]]) <= bw, , drop = FALSE]
  in_bw$D <- as.integer(in_bw[[running_col]] >= 0)
  in_bw$r <- in_bw[[running_col]]
  in_bw$r_interact <- in_bw$r * in_bw$D
  model <- lm(as.formula(paste(outcome_col, "~ r + D + r_interact")), data = in_bw)
  tid <- broom::tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "D")
  list(
    tau   = tid$estimate,
    se    = tid$std.error,
    ci_lo = tid$conf.low,
    ci_hi = tid$conf.high,
    n     = nrow(in_bw)
  )
}

text:
2. E-Value — Unmeasured Confounding Sensitivity
The E-value (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017) answers:

“How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be (in terms of its association with both treatment and outcome) to fully explain away the observed effect?”

A large E-value means the result is robust to unmeasured confounding.
Formula for OR:
E-value = OR + sqrt(OR * (OR - 1))     if OR >= 1
E-value = 1/OR + sqrt(1/OR * (1/OR - 1))  if OR < 1

# Fit adjusted model
model_adj <- glm(
  mi ~ statin + age + smoking + chd_history + ldl_baseline + ses_score,
  data = df, family = binomial()
)
tid_statin <- broom::tidy(model_adj, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "statin")
adj_or   <- tid_statin$estimate
adj_or_lo <- tid_statin$conf.low
adj_or_hi <- tid_statin$conf.high

evalue_or <- function(OR) {
  if (OR >= 1) {
    OR + sqrt(OR * (OR - 1))
  } else {
    inv <- 1 / OR
    inv + sqrt(inv * (inv - 1))
  }
}

cat(sprintf("Adjusted OR for statin: %.3f\n", adj_or))

Adjusted OR for statin: 0.372

Verbal interpretation of sensitivity statistics:

-- Partial R2 of the treatment with the outcome: an extreme confounder (orthogonal to the covariates) that explains 100% of the residual variance of the outcome, would need to explain at least 0.67% of the residual variance of the treatment to fully account for the observed estimated effect.

-- Robustness Value, q = 1: unobserved confounders (orthogonal to the covariates) that explain more than 7.86% of the residual variance of both the treatment and the outcome are strong enough to bring the point estimate to 0 (a bias of 100% of the original estimate). Conversely, unobserved confounders that do not explain more than 7.86% of the residual variance of both the treatment and the outcome are not strong enough to bring the point estimate to 0.

Conversely, unobserved confounders that do not explain more than 5.27% of the residual variance of both the treatment and the outcome are not strong enough to bring the estimate to a range where it is no longer 'statistically different' from 0, at the significance level of alpha = 0.05.

3. Overlap & Positivity Assessment

# Estimate PS
ps_model <- glm(
  as.formula(paste("statin ~", paste(COVARIATES, collapse = " + "))),
  data = df, family = binomial()
)
df$ps <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

ps_min_treated <- min(df$ps[df$statin == 1])
ps_max_control <- max(df$ps[df$statin == 0])
in_support  <- df$ps >= ps_min_treated & df$ps <= ps_max_control
pct_support <- mean(in_support) * 100

p_ps <- ggplot(df, aes(ps, fill = factor(statin))) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ps_min_treated, xmax = ps_max_control,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#16A34A", alpha = 0.10) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "#2563EB", "1" = "#DC2626"),
    labels = c("Control", "Treated"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Propensity score",
    y = "Density",
    title = sprintf("PS Distribution: Overlap Check (common support %.0f%%)", pct_support)
  )

# IPTW weight distribution
df$w_ate <- ifelse(
  df$statin == 1,
  1 / pmin(pmax(df$ps, 0.05), 0.95),
  1 / (1 - pmin(pmax(df$ps, 0.05), 0.95))
)

p_w <- ggplot(df, aes(w_ate, fill = factor(statin))) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "#2563EB", "1" = "#DC2626"),
    labels = c("Control", "Treated"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "IPTW weight",
    y = "Density",
    title = sprintf("IPTW Weight Distribution (max=%.1f)", max(df$w_ate))
  )

# Effective sample size vs trimming threshold
trim_thresholds <- seq(0.05, 0.40, length.out = 30)
ess_vals <- vapply(trim_thresholds, function(t) {
  df_trim <- df[df$ps >= t & df$ps <= 1 - t, ]
  n <- nrow(df_trim)
  w_t <- df_trim$statin * 1 / pmin(pmax(df_trim$ps, t), 1 - t)
  (n^2) / ((sum(w_t)^2) / n)
}, numeric(1))
ess_df <- tibble(threshold = trim_thresholds, ess = ess_vals)

p_ess <- ggplot(ess_df, aes(threshold, ess)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#16A34A", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "PS trimming threshold",
    y = "Effective sample size",
    title = "Effective Sample Size vs Trimming"
  )

p_overlap <- p_ps + p_w + p_ess
print(p_overlap)







ggsave(file.path(mod06_dir, "overlap_positivity.png"), p_overlap,
       width = 16, height = 4, dpi = 120)

# Test 1: Placebo outcome — an outcome that should NOT be affected by treatment
# Eye color should not be caused by statin use!
set.seed(5)
df$eye_color <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.35)  # purely random

placebo_mod <- glm(
  as.formula(paste("eye_color ~ statin +", paste(COVARIATES, collapse = " + "))),
  data = df, family = binomial()
)
placebo_or <- exp(unname(coef(placebo_mod)[["statin"]]))
cat("Placebo outcome test (eye color ~ statin):\n")

              "PASS: no spurious effect" else "FAIL: unexplained association!"))

# Test 2: Random treatment permutation — break any true causal effect
set.seed(42)
permutation_ors <- numeric(200)
placebo_form <- as.formula(paste("mi ~ statin_perm +", paste(COVARIATES, collapse = " + ")))
for (i in seq_len(200)) {
  df_perm <- df
  df_perm$statin_perm <- sample(df$statin)
  lr_perm <- glm(placebo_form, data = df_perm, family = binomial())
  permutation_ors[i] <- exp(unname(coef(lr_perm)[["statin_perm"]]))
}

perm_or_null <- permutation_ors
p_perm <- mean(perm_or_null <= adj_or)

text:
6. Knowledge Check

E-value = 2.1 for your statin analysis. Is this large or small? What known confounders (e.g. healthy user bias) have RRs in this range?
Your PS distribution shows poor overlap for elderly patients (age >80). What are your options?
The permutation p-value is 0.001. What does this tell you about the observed association?
A placebo outcome (baseline albumin from before statin initiation) shows OR=1.12. Should you be concerned?
Calculate Rosenbaum’s gamma (how much unmeasured confounding would change the conclusion) using a simple sign test.


# Exercise 5 — simplified Rosenbaum gamma bound
# For a binary outcome, test how much gamma (odds of differential unmeasured confounding)
# would be needed to make the result non-significant

# Use matched pairs analysis (simplified)
# In matched pairs, under gamma=1 (no hidden bias), we expect binomial with p=0.5
set.seed(42)
# Find pseudo-matched pairs (PS matching)
simple_match <- function(df, ps_col = "ps", treatment = "statin") {
  treated <- df[df[[treatment]] == 1, ]
  control <- df[df[[treatment]] == 0, ]
  treated <- treated[order(treated[[ps_col]]), ]
  control <- control[order(control[[ps_col]]), ]
  n_pairs <- min(nrow(treated), nrow(control))
  list(
    y_t = treated$mi[seq_len(n_pairs)],
    y_c = control$mi[seq_len(n_pairs)]
  )
}

pairs <- simple_match(df)
y_t <- pairs$y_t
y_c <- pairs$y_c
# Discordant pairs (pairs where outcome differs)
disc <- y_t != y_c
n_disc <- sum(disc)
n_treated_wins <- sum((y_t < y_c) & disc)  # treated has LOWER MI rate
cat(sprintf("Discordant pairs: %d | Treated outcome better: %d\n",
            n_disc, n_treated_wins))

Discordant pairs: 80 | Treated outcome better: 40

# Under gamma=1: test statistic ~ Binomial(n_disc, 0.5)
p_gamma1 <- pbinom(n_treated_wins, n_disc, 0.5)  # one-sided
cat(sprintf("p-value at gamma=1 (no hidden bias): %.6f\n", p_gamma1))

p-value at gamma=1 (no hidden bias): 0.544464

# Find gamma that makes p = 0.05
p_at_gamma <- function(gamma) {
  p_plus <- gamma / (1 + gamma)
  pbinom(n_treated_wins, n_disc, p_plus) - 0.05
}

gamma_threshold <- tryCatch(
  uniroot(p_at_gamma, interval = c(1, 10))$root,
  error = function(e) NA_real_
)
if (!is.na(gamma_threshold)) {
  cat(sprintf("Gamma threshold (Rosenbaum): %.2f\n", gamma_threshold))
  cat(sprintf("  Unmeasured confounding must change treatment odds by >%.2f-fold\n",
              gamma_threshold))
  cat("  to make the result non-significant at alpha=0.05\n")
} else {
  cat("Result is robust to extreme levels of unmeasured confounding (gamma > 10)\n")
}

Gamma threshold (Rosenbaum): 1.48
  Unmeasured confounding must change treatment odds by >1.48-fold
  to make the result non-significant at alpha=0.05

2. Spatial Data Structures in Health Analytics








Type

Key CRS concepts: - WGS 84 (EPSG:4326): latitude/longitude in degrees — for global data - NAD83 (EPSG:4269): North American datum — for US health data - Albers Equal Area (EPSG:5070): preserves area — for choropleth maps
A choropleth map is a thematic map in which geographic regions are shaded in proportion to a statistical variable (disease rates, population density, income). In health analytics, choropleths visualise the geographic distribution of outcomes, risk factors, or access to care across counties, states, or census tracts.

text:
4. Classification Schemes for Health Maps
There are multiple ways to classify continuous values into categories for health maps:

Equal interval: Divides the range of data into categories with equal-sized intervals.
Quantile: Splits the data so that each class contains the same number of observations (e.g. quintiles).
Natural Breaks (Jenks): Groups values to minimise within-class variance and maximise between-class differences.


n_classes <- 5
vals <- gdf$diabetes_prev

brks_equal <- classIntervals(vals, n = n_classes, style = "equal")
brks_quant <- classIntervals(vals, n = n_classes, style = "quantile")
brks_jenks <- classIntervals(vals, n = n_classes, style = "jenks")

classify_map <- function(gdf_in, brks, title) {
  gdf_in$class <- cut(gdf_in$diabetes_prev, breaks = brks$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
  ggplot(gdf_in) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
    scale_fill_brewer(name = "Prevalence (%)", palette = "RdYlGn", direction = -1) +
    labs(title = paste("Diabetes %:", title)) +
    theme_map()
}

p_eq <- classify_map(gdf, brks_equal, "Equal Interval")
p_q  <- classify_map(gdf, brks_quant, "Quantile (quintiles)")
p_j  <- classify_map(gdf, brks_jenks, "Natural Breaks (Jenks)")

p_class <- (p_eq | p_q | p_j) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Classification Scheme Comparison — Adult Diabetes Prevalence")
print(p_class)







ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "classification_schemes.png"), p_class,
       width = 18, height = 5, dpi = 150)

  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, colour = "#2563EB") +

text:
6. Spatial Join — Linking Point Data to Polygons
Simulate hospital locations as points, place them inside county polygons (weighted by uninsured count as a population-size proxy), then join each hospital to the containing county. Overlay hospitals on a PCP-supply map and check the ecological correlation with diabetes.

set.seed(13)
N_HOSPITALS <- 400
weights <- pmax(gdf$n_uninsured, 1)
weights <- weights / sum(weights)
hosp_idx <- sample.int(nrow(gdf), N_HOSPITALS, replace = TRUE, prob = weights)

# Place each hospital randomly inside its assigned county polygon
place_in_poly <- function(geom) {
  bb <- st_bbox(geom)
  for (i in 1:20) {
    pt <- st_sfc(st_point(c(runif(1, bb["xmin"], bb["xmax"]),
                            runif(1, bb["ymin"], bb["ymax"]))),
                 crs = st_crs(geom))
    if (as.logical(st_within(pt, geom, sparse = FALSE))) return(pt[[1]])
  }
  st_centroid(geom)[[1]]
}

hosp_geoms <- lapply(hosp_idx, function(i) place_in_poly(gdf$geometry[i]))

title: Choropleth Mapping
text:
7. Knowledge Check

A choropleth map uses quantile classification and shows your county in the highest quintile. A colleague uses equal-interval and shows it in the 4th class. Which is “correct”?
SPR = 1.45 for a rural county (diabetes / national mean). What does this mean, and what information do you need to know if this is statistically significant?
You want to map diabetes prevalence for census tracts. Your denominator (population) comes from the 2020 Census but your numerator covers 2018–2022. What are the key assumptions?
The correlation between PCP count and diabetes prevalence is negative. A colleague concludes “more doctors reduce diabetes.” What fallacy is this?
Compute a bivariate choropleth: classify counties into 3×3 cells by both obesity and diabetes prevalence, and colour-code the 9 combinations.


# Exercise 5 — Bivariate choropleth (3x3 = 9 classes)
obesity_cat <- as.integer(cut(gdf$pct_obesity,
                              breaks = quantile(gdf$pct_obesity, probs = 0:3 / 3),
                              include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)) - 1
diab_cat <- as.integer(cut(gdf$diabetes_prev,
                           breaks = quantile(gdf$diabetes_prev, probs = 0:3 / 3),
                           include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)) - 1
gdf$bivariate_class <- obesity_cat * 3 + diab_cat

biv_colors <- c(
  "Ob:Low Diab:Low"  = "#e8e8e8", "Ob:Low Diab:Med"  = "#dfb0d6", "Ob:Low Diab:High"  = "#be64ac",
  "Ob:Med Diab:Low"  = "#ace4e4", "Ob:Med Diab:Med"  = "#a5add3", "Ob:Med Diab:High"  = "#8c62aa",
  "Ob:High Diab:Low" = "#5ac8c8", "Ob:High Diab:Med" = "#5698b9", "Ob:High Diab:High" = "#3b4994"
)
ob_lbl <- c("Low", "Med", "High")
db_lbl <- c("Low", "Med", "High")
lab_map <- sprintf("Ob:%s Diab:%s", ob_lbl[floor(0:8 / 3) + 1], db_lbl[(0:8) %% 3 + 1])
gdf$biv_lab <- factor(lab_map[gdf$bivariate_class + 1], levels = names(biv_colors))

p_biv <- ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = biv_lab), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = NULL, values = biv_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Bivariate Choropleth: Adult Obesity × Diabetes Prevalence",
    subtitle = "light = low/low, dark = high/high"
  ) +
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(p_biv)

2. OLS Baseline and Diagnostic Tests
OLS model: \(\mathrm{diabetes}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \mathrm{obesity}_i + \beta_2 \cdot (\%\ \mathrm{aged\ 65+})_i + \beta_3 \cdot \mathrm{uninsured}_i + \varepsilon_i\)
Obesity is the focal behavioural risk factor. Percent aged 65+ adjusts for age structure. Uninsured count is a County Health Rankings access/size proxy. (Do not put SPR on the right-hand side: SPR is diabetes / national mean, a rescaling of the outcome.)

Decision rule (Anselin 1988; Anselin et al. 1996):

If only the LM lag test is significant → fit a Spatial Lag Model.
If only the LM error test is significant → fit a Spatial Error Model.
If both are significant, compare the robust LM statistics and choose the larger one.
If neither is significant, OLS is adequate (no residual spatial structure after covariates).

title: Spatial Regression: Lag, Error & GWR
text:
3. Spatial Regression
Sometimes, data from nearby locations are similar just because they are close to each other. Ordinary regression (\(y = X\beta + \mathrm{error}\)) assumes observations are independent. With maps and spatial data, that is often not true.
Spatial regression methods fix this by adding geography into the regression model.
There are two main types:

Spatial Lag Model (SLM)

This model assumes your outcome (\(y\)) depends not just on your own characteristics (\(X\)), but also on the outcome in nearby areas.

Spatial Error Model (SEM)

Instead of \(y\) depending on neighbours, this model says the errors are spatially correlated. If the regression misses something in one area, it probably misses it nearby too.


So, spatial regression makes sure you’re not ignoring geography, and tries to avoid the problem of “neighbours being similar just because they’re neighbours”.
(In simple terms, imagine house prices: your house value depends on your house’s properties and on the prices of houses nearby. The same logic applies to county diabetes rates.)
We fit both models with spatialreg (maximum likelihood). Do not grid-search \(\rho\) or \(\lambda\) by forming dense \(|I - \rho W|\) determinants on 3,108 counties — that is \(O(n^3)\) per candidate and is exactly what lagsarlm() / errorsarlm() already do efficiently.

3.1 Spatial Lag Model (SLM)
The Spatial Lag Model (SLM) understands that things nearby tend to influence each other.
Imagine you want to predict diabetes prevalence in different counties. In normal regression, we assume each county is independent. But what if nearby counties’ rates affect each other?
The SLM makes your prediction depend on both the usual factors and the values in surrounding places. Think: a county’s diabetes rate depends not only on its own obesity and age structure, but also on diabetes in neighbouring counties (spillover, shared culture, shared food environment).
The SLM equation:
\[
y = \rho\, W y + X\beta + \varepsilon
\]
Where:

\(y\) = outcome (diabetes prevalence)
\(X\) = predictors (obesity, % aged 65+, uninsured)
\(\beta\) = regression coefficients
\(W\) = spatial weights (who is a neighbour)
\(\rho\) (rho) = how much neighbours’ values matter
\(Wy\) = spatial lag (“neighbourhood average” of \(y\))
\(\varepsilon\) = residual noise

In plain language: “My value is influenced by my neighbours’ values, plus my own characteristics, plus some randomness.”

# SLM: y = rho W y + X beta + e  — spatialreg::lagsarlm
# method = "Matrix" avoids a dense eigen-decomposition of the 3108 × 3108 weights
slm <- lagsarlm(
  diabetes_prev ~ pct_obesity + pct_65plus + n_uninsured,
  data = gdf, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE, method = "Matrix", quiet = TRUE
)
print(summary(slm, Nagelkerke = TRUE))
